SOLDIERS IN THE HARVEST FIELDS.
MR. CARDWELL'S letter to the Secretary of
the Trades Council may be taken as satis-
factory so far as it goes. To working men the
subject is a most serious one, one in regard to
which their vigilance should never be relaxed.
It must not be forgotten that amongst those
to whom the Government of the country is
entrusted, class interests operate and class
prejudices almost necessarily exist. In the
past the interests of labour have suffered
sorely in consequence of this, but now that
the working people have gained possession of
political power, now that they really can
influence the conduct of those in authority,
they would be the agents of their own dis-
honour and loss, if they did not manfully
protest against any and every form of wrong
attempted to be practised against them, come
from where it may.
In looking at the present condition of things
as between employer and employed, it may be
said that whilst there is much to be pleased
with, there is much also calculated to beget
anxiety and fear. There can be no doubt
that the existence of trades societies, and the
discipline and self-reliance they have given
our workers, have greatly lessened the danger
from outbreaks of violence, which at one
time were the probabilities of almost any day
or hour. It is true that in our largo towns
there are numbers of people upon whom no
certain reliance can be placed, and it is to be
feared that under severe pressure through bad
trade or any other painful cause, turbulence
and riot might be looked for almost with cer-
tainty. But without the co-operation of the
intelligent portion of the working men, the
action of these could have no definite pur-
pose, and, therefore, would not permanently
disturb the existing order of things.
in the agricultural districts matters are very
different. There the people have been suffering
deep distress for generations. Their quietness
has been the result of want of thought,
absence of plan, or hope of union for the pur-
pose of joint action with a view to its remedy.
They are now moving, and whether they
understand the strength of their own case
or not, they do feel that it is a good one.
So far the outside public have strongly
sympathised with them, and what is of more
importance than anything else the workers of
• the great towns are thoroughly and enthusi-
astically on their side. People really do not
care about the peddling disputes raised by the
farmers and their friends, as to whether wages
amount to 10s., 125., or 13s. per week, with
or without perquisites. Taking wages at the
highest figure, at which they have been put.
they are scandalously and shamefully low.
Figure out the sums stated, as we may,
nobody can see, even in the largest amount, the
means of supporting a family in decency and
comfort; and in the presence of the bound-
less luxury and extravagant waste of the

fight between the agricultural labourer and
the farmer has this most dangerous element
removed from it, and before the next harvest
is ready for the sickle it is to be hoped that a
gradual improvement in the men's wages and
general conditions of life will be made. Added
to other things, emigration is doing its work.
Labourers will not, in a short time, be so
thick on the ground, and landlords and
farmers will, at least, have begun to find out
that their gains must not be made by starving
the peasant out of the country, or into his
grave. Necessity is a stern and imperative
teacher, which even English landlords must
listen to if they would avoid a collision, in
which they would be the chief sufferers what-
ever its issue.

LLOYD JONES.

articles.title: AGRICULTURAL LABDURERS.
articles.text:
AGRICULTURAL LABDURERS.

To all appearance the agricultural labourer
will influence political action next session, by
the necessity of permanently improving
his condition as cultivator of the soil,
which cannot be done under the present
land tenure. The hiws of primogeniture
and entail stand in the way; the land
is locked up among too few proprietors.
It is not only divided among too few, but it
is looked up by those laws among that few as
if it never could, or ought to be changed,
which is, no doubt, the opinion of the Duke
of MARLBOROUGH: and the Bishop of GLOUCES-
TER', that is, if either of these persons have
sense enough to have an opinion on the
matter. The Bisuor's reply to the ATTORNEY-
GENERAL, complaining of" being slandered,
greatly slandered," for saying that which, in the
act of denying, he owned to, is evidence that
he, at least, has not. He may have a strong
animal instinct grounded in a hazy sort of
way on the interest of his class, or what he
believes to be its interest, and on native
stupidity, but rational opinion ho can have
none, for what opinion can a ruan have who
owns to what he said while in the net of
denying that he said it ?—as he does in the
matter of the horsepond ; or, allowing that he
has an opinion, what is it worth ? It is to be
deplored that a man of so low a mental calibre
should be invested with a high dignity in the
church, and still more that he should be in-
vested by that dignity with a seat in the Upper
House of Legislature. This is only reArred
to to point out the low state mentally of some
of those who would keep these labourers, be-
cause they are labourers, down to the position
of serfs, and expect them to be thankful that
they are serfs, and grateful to their masters
for treating them as slaves. It is only the
mournful fact that these, and such as these, are
invested ,with a voice potential in legislating
on such matters that justifies the mention of
them at all.

The Daily Teleyrvli, of Nov. 21, comment-
ing on the meeting that is to take place in
Exeter Hall the second Tuesday in next
month in an admirable article puts the ques-
tion in its true form in the following words :
"Is the agricultural labourer to be regarded as
a member of the working classes? and if so, is he
not entitled to wages as good, and treatment as
liberal, as are accor&d—we will not say to a
skilled artizan—but to the factory hand, and the
day labourer Is a husbandman—man for lu ifl
and work for work—as good as a railway porter,
or a bricklayer's hod carrier? If he be so, has he
not a right to commensurate pay? If he be not,
the sooner we are candid enough to rivet an iron

swineherd and born thrall, was treated, the better
it might be for the purpose of correctly defining
the various grades in the community
We earnestly hope that the working men *ho
arc to meet next month will be invited to express
a distinct opinion whether the end of a long life of
toil—a life in which the wages of the toiler have
rarely been more than sufficient to keep body and

We endorse the whole article, but especially
that part of it we have quoted. It is pre.=
cisely the same as the state of things which
ushered in, and in a main degree caused, the
French Revolution of 1793, and the sweeping
away of the French landlords, lay and
clerical, which followed. We do not think
that the same catastrophe will take place here,
because we are of opinion that the cause will be
removed; that the land tenure will be changed,
and this tenure will be made so as to allow
proper wages to be given. But when we con-
sider that it resolves itself into a pecuniary
sacrifice to be paid by the landlord and farmer,
and when we consider the meanness and
rapacity of which these classes have been
capable in times that are byegone, of openly
getting the wages of these labourers paid out

Let there be emigration, molt as I hear is

labourers are the right stuff; they are the sort
that will succeed, as the pauper emigrants
were the wrong sort. There will be no failure
here. The more that are willing to go the
better. Make a dearth of agricultural
labourers; by this means the feudal tenure of
land will be loosened, and the way paved to
the breaking of it up, by the repeal of the
laws of primogeniture and entail. An exodus
of this class, while it will benefit those who
go even beyond their hope, will compel the
landlord and the farmer to do justice to those
who remain, and judging from the past
they need a gentle compulsion to do simple
justice even when it is ultimately their own
interest to do so. But it is to this remedy
that attention must be directed, and upon its
practicability will the permanent issue of the
result depend. Let there be a dearth of
agricultural labourers, by an exodus of emi-
grants, and their cause and their future well-
being is safe. The agricultural gang system
shows what the squires and farmers are
capable of; but a dearth of labourers will en-
sure good wages and good treatment, and will
force on the Government an alteration in the
land tenure, whereby the land may be made
to produce more, and the laws of primogeni-

THE WORKMEN'S_ PEA.CE ASSO-

CIATION.

A conference of representative working men,
convened by the Workmen's Peace Association,
was held on Tuesday in the Mechanics'
Institution, David-street, Manchester, for the
purpose of considering the best means of sup-
-Porting the proposal which is to be made in
the next session of Parliament to substitute
international arbitration for war. There was
a large attendance of delegates from Lancashire,
Yorkshire, and Cheshire. Mr. Bailey, secre-
tary of the Preston Trades Council, was
appointed chairman, and Mr. Corbett, of Old-
ham, secretary, of the conference.
The Chairman said it had been thought
desirable by the Council of the Peace Associa-
tion in Loudon that an expression of opinion
should be given on this important question.
As a majority of the delegates were officials
()Collected with large and important trade
societies, and had for a number of years
favoured arbitration aid concilation in pre-
ference to strikes, they believed that arbitra-
tion was a just, honest, and fair principle, and
could be carried out in international as well
as trade disputes.
Mr. Cremer, general secretary of the Council
of the Association, said the Workmen's Peace
Association was formed out of a cotnmitee that
was appointed during the Franco-Prussian
Witr.

Mr. Pritchard, Liverpool, moved
That the commercial and economical advance-
rnent of the industrial classes being essential to
their intellectual and moral development, and as
war between nations diminishes production, in-
creases the cost of food, entails heavy financial
burdens, dehumanises, retards national progress,
and does t permanently settle disputes between
nations, one war generally begetting another, this
Conference gives its hearty adhesion to the principle
of international arbitration as a practical, rational,
and economical moans of permanently settling in-
ternational disputes, and expressos its fervent hope
that the House of Commons will give a cordial
support to to motion which Mr. 11. Richard has
notified his intention of moving in the next session
of Parliament, which motion has for its object the
framing of a code of international law and the
permanent establishment of an international
tribunal. .

Mr. J. Bell, Birkenhead, seconded the
resolution, which having been supported by
Mr. Mottershead;London, and other delegates,
was passed.
Mr. Knight, secretary of the Liverpool
Boiler Makers' Association, moved :
That this Conference gives its adhesion and sup-
port to the principle of international arbitration
quite independently of party politics, believing that
the principle involves interests of such magnitude
as to raise it above class or party, and in this
spirit urges the electors of the United Kingdom to
make the question one of the tests of a candidate's
fitness to represent them in Parliament, believing
that when this is done the House of Commons
will soon discover means to overcome the obstacles
which are said to exist and to a practical ap-
plication of the principle.
Mr. Banks, secretary of the Spinners' Insti-
tute Preston, seconded the resolution.
Mr. M'Donald, of the House Painters'
Alliance, Manchester, Mr. P. Shorrocks, Man-
chester, and several other speakers supported
the resolution,which was passed.
Mr. Whalley, Blackburn, proposed, and Mr.
L. Wood, Stockport, seconded—
That for the purpose of bringing the question
prominently before the electors of Lancashire,
Yorkshire, and Cheshire, we pledge ourselves to
use our influence in our respective localities and
among our own order in promulgating the views
set forth in the foregoing resolution; and, further,
we urge the necessity of bolding a series of public
meetings in the boroughs of the above-mentioned
districts.

The resolution was passed.
On the motion of Mr. Corbett, Oldham,
seconded by Mr. Hamson, Huddersfield, a re-
solution was passed expressing the approval
of the Conference of the plan suggested by the
Association for the establishment of a High
Court of Nations.

Mr. B. Tattersall, ltoyton, proposed—
That nine members be appointed a committee
to carry into effect the resolutions adopted by the
Conference, and to co.operato with the central
body in London, such committee being authorised
to receive subscriptions for the purposes of the
public meetings and ether expenses attending its
peaceful thissicin.
The resolution was seconded by Mr. Sewell,
Bradford, and was passed.
The committee having been appointed, the
Conference passed a vote of thanks to the
Chairman, which concluded the proceedings.

articles.title: METROPOLITAN POLIOE.
articles.text:
THE METROPOLITAN POLIOE.

meeting of sympathy with the discharged
members of the Metropolitan Police was held in
Hyde-park on Sunday afternoon, Mr. Odger pre-
siding. The only police speaker was ex-constable
Goodchild, whe stated that the action of the
authorities were unjust and cruel, and not in ac-
cordance with the usages which ordinarily exist
between employer and employed. A memorial
was adopted to the Home-office asking for the re-
lease and reinstatement of the offending police-
men, and the following resolutions were proposed,
seconded, and carried :

1. That this meeting views with deep regret the
conduct of the authorities in summarily suspend-
ing and dismissing efficient and well-tried ser-
geants and constables of the police force without
offering to meet them upon fair and reasonable
conditions, thereby jeopardising the place- and
safety of the community, and declares that when
off duty, constables have as much right to meet
and discuss questions affecting their own and the
public interests, as any other portion of the British
people.
2. That this meeting is of opinion that the sum-
mary dismissal of members of the police force is
unjust and cruel, and that while a month's notice
is required from each and all of them, it is only
fair, and in accordance with usages which ordinarily
exist between employers and employed, that the
men should have a month's notice also.

articles.title: AMALGAMATED SOCIETY OF RAILWAY CARRIAGE AND WAGGON OPERATIVES.
articles.text:
AMALGAMATED SOCIETY OF RAIL-
WAY CARRIAGE AND WAGGON
OPERATIVES.

A meeting was held last Saturday at the Drovers'
Antis, Openshaw, near Manchester, for the purpose
of forming a branch; delegates attended from
Miles Platting Branch, and Earlstown Waggon
Makers' Society. Mr. Ogden took the chair, and
in a very excellent speech detailed the advantages
of combination.

,
Mr. Toogood, Vice-President, Platting Branch,
spoke on the advantages of all the trades con-
nected with the railway carriage and waggon
departments combining; together:and co-operating
with the Railway. Servants' Society in regard to
emigration and other schemes, and the advantage
of the United Kingdom Society of Coachmakers
co-operating with them likewise.
Mr. Jackson, Vice-President, Earlstown Society,
was of opinion that the branch should consist of
waggon makers alone. It was decided to start a
branch in connection with Platting and Birming-
ham, to consist for the present, of railway body
and carriage makers, coach finishers and waggon
makers, but it is very probable that other trades
connected with the railway carriage and waggon
departments will be admitted shortly.

articles.title: TRUCK SYSTEM.
articles.text:
THE TRUCK SYSTEM.

On Tuesday the Council of the Society of Frame-
work Knitters of Notts, Leicestershire, and
Derbyshire, mot at Nottingham, and there was a
large attendance of delegates. The principal
business Was to consider the extent and evils of
the truck system and the best means for its
abolition; and the Council unanimously resolved
to petition Parliament in favour of a measure
having such abolition for its object. A deputation
from the Council then waited upon Mr. A. J.
Mundella, M.P. for Sheffield, drawing his attention
to the matter, and urging him, in case the Govern-
ment should fail to bring in a Bill for the abolition
of the truck system, to introduce a Bill himself.
After listening to the various representations of
the deputation, Mr. Mundella promised to bring in
a Bill as requested in case the Government
declined or neglected to do so. This announce-
ment was afterwards reported to the Council, and
received with loud cheering by the assembled
deputies.

articles.title: LONDON COSTERMONGERS.
articles.text:
THE LONDON COSTERMONGERS.

. On Sunday afternoon a numerously-attended
meeting was held at Billingsgate Market of the
class of costermongers who retail fried fish, &c.,
to protest against a system of fraud which they
allege they have been subjected to for a long time
past. The principal speaker was a cestermonger
named Benjamin Hart, and the meeting was also
addressed by a " eoster" of the name of Nickham
by another, fart, and by one or two other mem-
bers of the same order.

It appears that every day at Billingsgate, after
the wholesale buyers have had the pick of the
market and departed, a large number of men who
are known in the trade as " smokers " make a rush
for all the leavings, and the competition which
daily takes place amongst them is so keen that the
salesmen, they allege, have taken advantage of
their eagerness to cheat them. The plaice which
has remaind unsold, and the mackerel and had-
docks, and other fish, which can he either carried
oF to the fish-shop in poor end populous districo,

and:fried to make cheap meals, or sent to the
" curers " to be converted into real" finnons," are
packed into "pads," and into deep round baskets,
which should hold, if properly filled, about two
bushels and a half, and are sold by auction. A
notice is at the same time prominently exhibited in
the market that "the fish is bought with all its
faults," and that "no money will be returned."
The speakers declared, and the meeting endorsed
the statements, that it had of late become an al-
most constant occurrence to find, upon opening ths
" peds " and other baskets after purchase, that
there was either a great quantity of ice stowed
away at the bottom of the packages, or the fish,
especially the plaice, were put in edgeways until
within a few layers of the top, and so the buyer
was seriously defrauded of his just weight. There
wore several fish salesmen present at the meeting,
but they offered no remarks, and in the end a
resolution was unanimously carried to the effect
that in future the fish disposed of in the way
described, and to this particular class of coster-
mongers, should be purchased only after having
been duly weighed and certified.

articles.title: BLACKBURN BRICKLAYERS.
articles.text:
THE BLACKBURN BRICKLAYERS.

Rather more than a fortnight since the opera-
tive bricklayers of Blackburn applied to the master
bricklayers, urging that the old rule of reducing
the scale of payment of wages during the winter
season might be discontinued, and asking that
they might be paid the same rate of wages in
winter as in summer so long as the weather was
light. The masters have refused to concede these
terms, consequently the operatives have come out
on strike.

articles.title: IRONWORKERS AT STOCK-
articles.text:
THE IRONWORKERS AT STOCK-

TON-CiN,TEES.

On Tuesday morning, the fitters, smiths, car-
penters and masons employed at the " Stockton
Rail Mill, the Malleable Ironworks, and the West
Stockton Ironworks struck work in consequence
of a dispute between them and their employers on
the wages question, which it is said had previously
been decided by the Board of Arbitration. It ap-
peared that the Board had decided that the men
were to have more money paid to them, and it was
expected by the men that they would receive the
same at the pay on Saturday last, but they were
refused. Hence the present action on their part.
What they anticipated receiving, and which it is
said
.has been paid by some employers in the
neighbouring towns, was something like 4s. in the
pound from July last. On Tuesday afternoon Mr.
Trow, one of the vice-presidents of the Board of
Arbitration, in the absence of Mr. J. Bane, of
Darlington, met the ironworkers of the Malleable
Iron Works and the Rail Mill at the Cambrian
Hotel, Stockton. Mr. Trow having heard the
statement of the men about the money due to them,
stated that the books should be examinel with a
view to them baying their rights, and after a
short time the men agreed to return to their work
and await the decision of the deputation appointed,
believing that they have put a right construction
on the previous decision of Mr. Kettle. With re-
ference to the puddlers at the Moor Ironworks,
where a dispute has been going on about the
quality of the coal used at the Works, the remainder
of the cases which were to have been heard on
Wednesday before the magistrates against the
men were adjourned until Friday.

articles.title: HARTLEPOOL BRICKLAYERS.
articles.text:
THE HARTLEPOOL BRICKLAYERS.

On Monday afternoon about 120 bricklayers and
their labourers, chiefly employed at and near the
West Hartlepool Rolling Mills, turned out on
strike on account of their employers' refusal to
entertain an application to adopt the same system
of diminished hours of labour recently conceded
by the master builders of Middlesborough to their
workmen.

TILURSDA.Y.—It is stated that the bricklayers of
West Hartlepool and their labourers have resumed
their employment on the original terms, viz.,
daylight to dusk—about eight hours per diem—
with one hour allowed for dinner,

articles.title: WEST YORKSHIRE MINERS.
articles.text:
THE WEST YORKSHIRE MINERS.

A meeting of colliers was held on Saturday
afternoon, in the Co-operative Hall, Normanton,
to consider the action of 31cssrs. Pope and Pearson,
of the West Riding Collieries, in discharging some
of their men in consequence (it is alleged) of their
having joined the Miners' union; and also to hear
addresses on the subject from Mr. McDonald,
president of the National Association of Miners,
and Mr. Councillor Northansell, of Barnsley, the
Vice-President. There was a crowded attendance;
the room was literally packed, and many were
unabla to gAia iidmittame. Mr. John Dixon,

secretary of the West Yorkshire Miners' Associa•
tion, was called to the chair.

The Chairman was loudly applauded on com-
mencing to speak. He described the position Of
affairs. Some months ago several colliers employed
by Messrs. Pope and Pearson expressed a desire
to join the West Yorkshire Miners' Association,
and they allied themselves with branches of the
same. They went on increasing in numbers till
there were between 200 and 300 of them in con-
nection with the union (there were now upwards
of 500 of them), and then they thought they ought
to have a check-weighman. They held a meeting
on the question, and Messrs. Pope and Pearson
hearing of it intimated that they would allow of
the appointment of two check-weighmen-006 for
each colliery. Two were chosen, and they went
to the machines, but were discharged from there.
Subsequently, one of them, whilst at the machine
asserting his right to be there as the men's repro- .
sentative, was taken, lodged in prison, and brought
before the magistrates charged with assaulting a
policeman who was paid by the proprietors of the
colliery. After that, by his (the chairman's) advice,
the men had not endeavoured to put a man on the
machine. That meeting was called to see whether ,
the men at Pope and Pearson's were determined to
have liberty, whether they still maintained a right
to join the union.
After Mr. A. McDonald had addressed the
meeting, Mr. Councillor Normaniell, secretary,
said that they had been trying to settle the question
without a disturbance, but in his opinion there wag
no way now but fighting. He did not believe in
strikes, but at times they wore necessary evils.
The Association would support the men there who
turned out for this principle. They would receive
a respectable sum per week, be kept out of debt,
and Messrs. Pope 'and Pearson and their managers,
Mr. Warburton and Mr. Hopkinson, would be
brought to see things in a new light.

A show of hands was then taken of those in the
room working at the West Riding collieries who
were for sticking to the union, and there was a
very large number of hands hold up, the result
being hailed with vociferous cheering.
On Monday evening the men in the employ of
Messrs. Pope and Pearson, West Riding collieries,
Altofts and Whitwood, near Wakefield, held a
meeting at Altofts for the purpose of deciding
whether to adhere to the Coalminers' Union, and
come out on strike, or to sever their connection
with the union and remain at work, 600 men em-
ployed by the firm being present. The men deter-
mined to send in fourteen days' notice on Thurs-
day. During the evening the men signed their
notices.

articles.title: NORTHERN IRONWORKERS.
articles.text:
THE NORTHERN IRONWORKERS.

Representatives of masters and men connected
with the iron trade in the North of England met
at Wolverhampton on Friday afternoon, before
Mr. Rupert Kettle, their arbitrator, and discussed
a point of difference arising out of the concession
of the employers in the North after the late ad-
vance of wages in South Staffordshire. Twenty-
five hundred workmen were affected by the deci-
sion. After two hours' discussion, there was
compromise and unanimous vote. This is a further
triumph for arbitration in trades disputes as esta-
blished by Mr. Kettle. The working of the deci-
sion will be to the advantage of the operatives
concerned, who are now placed under what ts
known as the ten per cent. average of the district.
Next year the classifying of ironworkers props
and workers in ironworks will be more complete.

THE AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS.

A meeting took place in the Corn Exchange,
Long Sutton, on Thursday last. Alderman Carter
and Mr. B. Taylor spoke. Ur. T. Banks occupied
the chair. _ _

Mr. B. Taylor, of Peterboro', addressed the meet-
ing, and was speaking for nearly an hour. He
commenced with claiming the sympathy and pity
of his hearers. He disclaimed any idea of gold
chains and black cloth coats, as well as the
insinuations that he understood followed—that the
poor working men paid for both. He fancied if
they tried it, they would find themselves very much
mistaken. He wished to state, too, that be was
not a paid man, that he went there, worked for
nothing, and "found" himself. He had been the
means of establishing some fifty branches of
labourers in and around Petarboro', and if any of
the Long Button friends went there they would
find the district well organized. Now he did not
think a man ought to be offended at being called a
"paid agitator." Every workman was worthy of
his hire, and no great movement was ever satis-
factorily carried out except somebody was ready
to speak and agitate in its behalf. He agreed
'with the Alderman that these working men got
a deal of fresh air, but it only reminded him
of the two men who discovered each other
out early one morning, one of whom was walk-
ing for the purpose of getting an appetite for
his breakfast, and the other a breakfast for his
appetite. He did not intend to take up a great
deal of their time, but ho wished to make them
understand that he did not think the farmers were
getting rich too soon, or that their profits were
exorbitant. But, he was prepared to make the
assertion that the agricultural labourers of the
country were not in their proper position—that
they were not properly paid, properly clothed,
properly housed, and properly educated. And ho
should like to hear it provSd to the contrary. He
was told in the Refreshment-room at the Spalding
station that the labourers were comfortable enough
before they (the agitators) came; and when asked
how he knew that, he replied that they could be
heard whistling at the plough, and that showed
they were happy. Well, he did not think that
was a proof, for he had heard of people who were
afraid of ghosts, whistling to keep their spirits up
(laughter). During an experience of forty years,
he never yet met an agricultural labourer who was
satisfied, and he held that there was not that good
feeling between the master and the man that
several of the farmers' friends would have them
believe. Now, he held that the working population
of the country were not in the position they ought
to be. When they considered that it was their
work, and toil, their sweat, and industry, that
produced the prosperity of the country, they were
not sufficiently remunerated.

articles.title: BELFAST BUILDING TRADES.
articles.text:
THE BELFAST BUILDING TRADES.

At Belfast there has recently been formed a
trades council, representing various operative
interests, whose functions are those of mediators
between roasters and men in matters of dispute,
and who are to correspond with the different
trades' councils of the 'United Kingdom, in order
that practical and efficient rules may be drawn up
for their guidance. .

At a meeting of this body in the Odd Fellows'
Hall, Belfast, on Saturday last, a dispute in which
the whole body of carpenters and joiners are
interested, engaged the almost exclusive attention
of the Council.
The Builders' Association had informed their
men that on and after Nov. 1 it was their inten-
tion to pay them by the hour. The wages of
carpenters and joiners would be—first-class, 6id.
per hour; second-class, 6td. When working out-
side in winter—first-class men, 7d.; second-class,
men, 61; with 11 hour for meals on the first five
days of the week, and one hour on Saturday. The
men had gone into work, to be paid the full time
of 64 hours per week, at 6fd, for first class men id.
per hour less. It was the general feeling of the
meeting that the dispute between the builders and
carpenters is not fully ripe for action to be taken
by the Council.
Next came the grievances of the stone-cutters,
The men were generally willing to work for 7d.
an hour during eight months of the year, and 71d.
during the four winter months, as during the
latter months their time would necessarily be
abridged by the darkness. The masters object to
the increased pay in winter. It was resolved that
the Council offer their services to settle the dispute
with the master builders and stone-cutters.

Then the bricklayers' complaints were enter-
tained. They have represented to the masters that
they object to, work by the bout, a 3 proposed.
Their argument is that, under the present system
they earn 28§i a week in the winter, and if they

are knocked off by the wet they can get leave to
work an extra quarter in fine weather to make up
for the loss; whereas, if they worked by the hour,
and they were knocked off at all they would lose
that hour. If they are unable to come to terms
with the masters, they will seek the sympathy and
assistance of the Trades' Council.

There appears to be a commendable desire
throughout the building trade in the North of
Ireland generally, on the side of the employers and
employed, to submit their disputes to arbitration
rather than adopt the suicidal policy of settling
their differences by strikes, which are pregnant of
disaster to all interests concerned.

articles.title: LIMESTONE MINERS AT
articles.text:
THE LIMESTONE MINERS AT

DUDLEY.

The dispute between the limestone miners and
employers entered upon a new phase on Wednes-
day morning. A largo number of the men in the
neighbourhood of Dudley Port and Great Bridge
went to work upon the faith of the compact
entered into with the employers some time ago
that they Should work eight hours per day only.
When in the various pits they were told by the
butties that nine hours would be the length a
time, or the stint of nine hours would have to be
done in the eight hours. The men all laid down
their tools and came up the pits. A mass meeting
of the men was held in Dudley, and it was un-
animously resolved to continue the nineteen weeks'
struggle.

THE CLYDE ENGINEERS.

men's demands, so that the fifty-one hours per
week, without any reduction of pay, has become
general over Scotland.

articles.title: WESTMINSTER WORKING MEN'S LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.
articles.text:
WESTMINSTER WORKING MEN'S
LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.

On Wednesday evening a meeting of working
men, presided over by Sir T. Powell Buxton; Was
hold at the Pimlieo Rooms, Warwick-street, at the
"Public inaugural meeting of the Westminster
Working Men's Association:" Among those present
were Mr. Thomas Hughes, "M.P., Mr. Mundella,
M.P., Mr. Arthur Arnold, Mr. G. Howell, Mr.
George Potter, Mr. Samos Baal, Mr. J. Crirr, Mr.
H. 13roadhurst, Mr. L. Hearn, and others. The
large room in'
.which the meeting was held was
full. Letters expressing regret, and not being
able to attend, but sympathising with the object,
were read from Right Hon. It. Lowe, M.P., Right
Hon. W. E. Forster, M.P., Right Hon. G. J. dos-
chen, M.P., Marquis of Hartington, M.P., Marquis
of Lansdowne, Mr. S. Morley, M.P., M. Julian
thldsmid, M.P., Professor Fawcett, M.P., Sir H.
Hoare, M.P., Mr. S. 13rogden, M.P., Sir Charles
Dilke, M.P., Mr. Walter Morrison, M.P., Hon.
Auberon Herbert, M.P., Lord Edmund Fitzmau-
rice, M.P., Sir John Bennett, and Mr. Edinund
Beales.

The Chaiimon, who was warmly received, in
opeeitii the proceedings, expressed the satisfaction
he felt in presiding at this inaugural meeting, but
at the same time felt surprised that it should have
been left to so late a date to establish a Liberal
Association in Wesiminster, the historic home of
Liberal politics. He was;however, glad to see it
established even now, and he hoped it would sub-
sist and flourish until it included every Liberal
elector in the district. It was proper that they
should be able to give a reason for the faith
that was in them, and to show why they sup-
ported Liberal principles and a Liberal Ministry.
(Cheers.) It was not necessary to go back 40
years, although during the whole of that time the
Liberal party had done good work; but let them
look merely at what a Liberal Government had
done during the last four years. In 1809 they
abolished the Irish Church; in 1870 they passed
a still more difficult Irish measure, the Land Act;
in 1871 they passed the Education Act, the good
effects of which were yet to be developed; and
this year the Scotch Education Bill. No doubt
they would deal with the land laws and those of
intestacy at an early date, and would most pro-
bably attempt to revise that salutary law of mort-
main which prevented land passing too freely into
the hands of religious corporations. There were
also the questions of local taxation and of legal
reform, which must be dealt with, but which
would reqatire careful consideration. They were
told that the Liberal party and its leaders were
becoming unpopular, and he admitted that one or
two members of the Liberal Government had com-
mitted acts which were calculated to render them
unpopular. Mr. Lowe, for instance, had taken a
violent party side down in Scotland on the Epping
Forest question, even whilst a Commission was
sitting, the object of which was to ascertain the
public rights aid to settle the question. He could
not admit the propriety of such conduct on the
'part of a prominent Minister of the Crown. (ITear,
hear.) Another ease of ministerial unpopularity
was, in his opinion, the fact that in some matters
the Liberal Government was in advance of its
time. They bad, for example, honestly accepted
the principle of international arbitration, but its
working at Geneva had not given satisfaction. He
trusted, however, that the people of England
would stick to that principle, and thus give an en-
lightened lead to tho other nations of the world.
(Hear, hear.) Having congratulated Ministers on
their having taken up the question of the slave
trade at Zanzibar; he concluded by calling on
wolking men to support the committee for the fur-
therance of which-the association was being formed.
(Loud cheers.)
Mr. George POtter, President of the Association,
then made a statement, in the course of which he
drew the working men's attention to the view
that their powers of influencing elections by
direct votes entailed upon them responsibilities.
These would be best fulfilled, he said, by their
being united. He spoke of the history of West-
minster in respect to the high class of men the
city in former days sent to Parliament, and he
contrasted the position of Radicalism when it was
associated with the name of Sir Francis Burdett
with the present times, when it was a great power
in the State. (Loud cheers.) The subscription to
the Association would be is. a year, and in the
course of the winter lectures would be given on
social and political subjects. They hoped to
secure the services of Sir Charles Dilko, Sir John
Bennett, Mr. Auberou Herbert, Mr. Arthur
Arnold, Mr. J. S. Mill, ind Professor Fawcett.
(Loud cheers.) The association would not pretend
to represent all the working men of Westminster;
but would leave the Conservative Working Men's
Association to 6 an its way rejoicing. Miny

of those present had worked hard, and had been
successful in elevating the position of the working
classes, and now it was time for them to help
themselves on further. (Cheers.) There was yet
work for them to do, and the working men should
at once be up and doing in preparation for the
next election, when there must be no neutrality,
but the recognition, without reserve or com-
promise, of the great principles of civil and re-
ligious liberty. (Applause.) Mr. Potter further
stated that it was his duty to inform the meeting
that two gentlemen, Mr. Mode Palmer, M.P., and
Captain Maxso, who had promised to attend the
meeting and speak, were not able to do so, but
they had sent the following letters which they
wished him to read.
Mr. Ilindo Palmer, M.P., wrote :

My Dear Sir,—l regret to find that having to
preside at a meeting at the Society of Art.B on the
subject of " Technical Education, I shall net be
able, as I intended, to be present at the West-
minster Working Men's Liberal Association. ,

My own return to Parliament by the spon-
taneous, unsolicited, and spirited action of the
working men of Lincoln, is a striking instance of
what may be accomplished by that body when
they are united, well combined, and determined
to effect their object.
Without organisation they are more like a
"rope of sand" than almost any other class of the
community.
I trust, therefore, that the working men of
Westminster will enrol themselves in largo num-
bers in the Westminster Liberal Association, and
thus, when the time comes they will be able to
make their strength felt, and insure a triumph for
the Liberal cause.
Captain Maxim wrote :

DEAIt regret much that t am compelled
to leave town to-morrow, and that I shall there-
fore be unable to attend the Westminster Working
Men's Liberal Association. I trust that the meet-
ing will be successful. I hope that an organiza-
tion of working men will be formed for the pur-
pose of influencing selection of candidate for next
election.

I have made up my mind only to vote for a
candidate who will pledge himself t ) support—
]. The National Education League Programme.

2. The Lend Tenure Reform Programme.

3. Electoral Representative Morin, based upon
proportional representation and the assimilation of
town and county franchise.
I hope some one will remind the meeting that
the population of Westminster entitles it to have
five members instead of two, and that under the
present shameful electoral system Lichfield and
Stamford, with a combined population of 15,000,
sends four Parliamentary representatives to the
two which are allotted to the quarter of a million
Inhabitants residing in Westminster.
I shall be prepared to subscribe to any move-
ment which may be started for the purpose of
bringing forward a candidate, even though he be
a "forlorn hope" candidate, who will stand upon
the above platform.
Mr. Gredy, joiner, moved the first resolution
That this meeting regards with satisfac-
tion the establishment of the Westminster
WorkingiNten's Liberal Association, and cordially
approves of its principles and objects; believing
such an organization to be necessary to enable the
working classes to exercise their legitimate in-
fluence in the political and municipal atf,iirs of the
constituency; and, therefore, heartily recommends
the Association to the support of the working
men of Westminster.

He said that the Constitutional Working Men's
Associations were said to go on more smoothly
than Liberal ones. Well, there was not much
among thorn to be divided about, for all they had
to do was to obey their superiors, and it appeared
to him that tho "working men" who belonged to
the "Constitutional Associations" were men who
were expecting or hoping for patronage or charity.
(If oar, and laughter.) He was not to be under-
stood as endorsing every mbasuro of' the present
Government, which had passed many measures
which were irritating to the working classes. It
was said that Government unpopularity was con-
fined to one or two individual members, but the fact

was that Government, as a whole, must take the
responsibility of the acts of all its members.
(Hear.) Their policy shoull not be, however, to
go over to the Tories, but rather compel a Liberal
Government to do Liberal work. (Cheers)

Mr. Morton, p tinter briefly seconded the resolu-
tion.

Mr. T. Hughes, M.P., supported the resolution,
and was received with cheers. Ho expressed his
satisfaction with the establishment and the objects
of the institution. It was high time, he said, that
somebody stirred among the Liberals, and if the
middle chss did not move, then it was good for
any ono who intended to do work in the future.
For his part he thought the working man hail a
fair shire of power. (N0,,n0.). But he said they
had, ainl it was only that they should poll together,
and then they might return whom they thought
fit. (Hear, hear.) Ho should be glad to see the
working Mtn united, but ho hoped not for °hiss
purposes. Ho thought they should unite with the
party owl with defined principles, and not with
narrow views. (Cheers.) Proceeding to speak on
questions which wore made class agitation's, he
reminded the Working men that Sir Powell Burton
lost his teat through bringing in thi Bill which

made Trades' Unions legal, and he hoped they
would remember that at the next election. Speak-
ing of the disunion of the Liberal party, he
referred to the manner in which the working men,
adopting the "cry" of leaders, had declared against

_
the Criminal Law Amendment Act, as a whole, an
Act, he said, which placed them in a much better
position than they would be if they were under the
old law, and what they should do would be
to go for the repeal of the picketing clauses
of the Act. In this, as in other cases, the de-
mand was made of a candidate to vote for one
particular thing. The fact was they went at it
like the bull in the china shop; one thing only
would suit them, and so disunion was caused.
There was another instance in the action of the
teetotalers on the licensing laws—it must be the
Permissive Bill, or nothing. Another question
which was made the cry of a small sect was the
repeal of the Contagious Diseases Act. Now, no
man with honesty, after reading the report of the
Royal Commission, could go in for the total repeal
of those Acts (cheers), and. yet the small section
who were for these would be satisfied with nothing
less. What the Liberal men of Westminster had
to do was to give and take, and not adopt any
pledge for any small section. (Cheers.)

_
Mr. Slundella, ALP., in supporting the motion,
was also received with cheers. He acknowledged
that Conservatiam could not have a milder type of
representative than Mr. W. IL Smith; but then,
ho said, it was to be remembered on any test ques-
tion that gentleman was always on the wrong side
of the voting list. He called upon them, too, to
remember that with Conservative government in
the past, when the population of England was ,
half what it was, starvation was everywhere in the
country, work was scarce, bread was dear, wages
low, and an increase of population was looked
upon as the greatest misfortune which could
occur. He declared that the principles of Cobden
and Bright had made the country what it was now,
and the future, he said, was still greater. It was
all very welt to mourn over what was lost in the
French Treaty, but let them look at the popula-
tion in this land which now took next to nothing
in our own manufactures—the agricultural la-
bourars ; for what, he asked, did that wretched
class in their present position consume of the work
of our cities, and yet with proper legislation that
class, 6,000,000 in number, would prove of more
value to our productions than a new country. He
spoke against the present land laws, the game
laws, and he said that when our country was
educated well, and governed well, it would be the
freest and happiest country in the world.
(Cheers.)

The resolution was carried unanimously.
Mr. Arthur Arnold moved the second resolu-
tion—

That, while this meeting rejoices in the for-
:nation of this Association in Westmin-
ster, it would also recognize the benefits
which have accrued to the working classes from
the nieasures secured to the coun.ry by the Liberal
petty ; and urges upon all true Liberals to adopt
concerted action at the next General Election to
secure a redistribution of seats, the assimilation of
the county to the borough franchise, a thorough
revision of the Land Laws, a reduction of the
national-expemliture, the direct representation of
labour in Parliament, end other great progressive
measures necessary for the trtie welfare of the
nation.

He advocated the redistribution of seats, the
assiindaVon of the county and borough frrnchises,
and the education of the rural population. The '
best way to promote their education would, in his
opinion, be, to give them the franchise. It was
the Reform Act of 1867 that carried the Education
Act. Lord Derby had in a recent speech, amid
many commonplace temarks, made one important
admission. He said that, with proper cultivation,
land might be m tde to double its present pro-
tduce. Let them remember that that meant
800 additional millions employed in the Imlay '-
ton of land. Improved land laws, along with
°doer progressive measures, were what the
working men should struggle for. (Cheers.)
He did not wish to throw abuse on the opposite
party. It was not right to expect that men whoin
proper place was behind the Liberals should be
able to enter in any way into those principles and
designs which constantly impelled the party to the
front. Liberalism was synonymous with civilisa-
tion itself. The true meaning of civilisation was
the extension of civil rights. Believing that pro-
gress was essential to humanity and was the Word
of God, he agreed with the last wofds spoken to
him by his friend Mr. Dufour, and commended
them to serious thought—" The golden age which
-mankind has placed in the past lies ever in the
future." (Loud cheers.)
Mr. J. Beal, in seconding the resolution, re-
minded Ms hearers of the past political history and
present situation of Westininstor ; anrl, while
giving credit to Mr. Smith as the best local mem-
ber they could have, he could not recommend him

as an Imperial representative, nor agree that he
should share the representation with a Libeial.
He warmly urged the Liberal working men of
Westminster to secure two seats at the next general
election. (Cheers.)
Mr. T. Carr moved a cordial vote of thanks to
the chairman, which was seconded by Mr. Lau-
rence Hearne, and carried by acclamation.

articles.title: MR. BRIGHT AND THE COMMERCIAL TREATY.
articles.text:
MR. BRIGHT AND THE COMMERCIAL
TREATY.

The following correspondence has been pub-
" 36, Bwanswell-street, Coventry, Nov. 20,
1872.

"Sin—ln carrying out the enclosed reso-
lution, passed at a public meeting in Coventry,
I was particularly directed to ask you if there
was any hope of the artisans of Coventry ob-
taining fair play in the fierce race of competi-
tion between France and England. We are
not aware that any class of her Majesty's sub-
jects have asked or demanded that the silk
trade of Coventry should be sacrificed to
enable them to obtain the ribbons of France
or Basle at one farthing per yard cheaper than
those manufactured in this country. If her
Majesty's Ministers did but know or consider
for one moment the vast amount of misery
and wretchedness these continued one-sided
and anti-free-trade treaties inflict upon seven
thousand industrious men and women in
Coventry, I do think they would hesitate
before they brought so great an evil upon us.
—I am, sir, yours respectfully,
" NATUANIET, POOLE."
"Llandudno, Nov. 22, 1872.
" is to be regretted that you and
your friends should distress yourselves about
the new treaty, and prefer, as I conclude you
would prefer, to have, no treaty at all. If
there were no treaty, the French Government
would not reduce their import duties, some of
them they would probably raise, and the
English Government would not impose new or
higher duties on importations from France.
The treaty, therefore, which fixes the limit of
the French tariff, but which does not prevent
its amendment in the direction of lower duties,
and which in no way affects the duties we
impose on foreign goods, can inflict no
injury on Coventry or on any other manufac-
turing town in the kingdom. The treaty may
not be a wise treaty on the part of France,
but it is impossible that it should be injurious
to England, for under its provisions England
does not bind herself to do anything which
I she would not willingly and wisely do if the
I treaty were not in existence. If, under the
treaty, the French tariff is in any degree lower
than it would be without the treaty then by
so much are we the gainers by it. Our
Government would have been delighted to
have signed a treaty under which the French
tariff would have been as liberal and as sensible
as our own, but it can only act for England,
and not for France. If lam not mistaken,
you were against the treaty of 1860, and on
the same grounds, doubtless, you are against
the renewed treaty of 1872. You think that
special interests of Coventry should have
been eared for at the expense of the general
population of the kingdom. But Irird
Granville is not the Minister for Coventry
only, but for the United Kingdom, and he and
his colleagues must act for the general good,
and not for any special interest or trade which
clamours for protection at his hands. In the
protest you have sent me you say that while
the French were fighting, in 1871, the trade
of Coventry was exceptionally good;' that is,
when you had no competition, your trade was
very good; and what you want now is, that
our tariff should prevent foreign competition
with you in this market, and give you pro-
sperity, at the cost of your customers, which
you had last year, caused by the calamities of
the French. am sorry, if not surprised, that
there are any working men in Coventry who
still think duties for protection are just and
good for English industry after the experience
of the last twenty-live years. Surely it is
something of a aiscredit to Coventry that,
almost alone among all the towns of the
United Kingdom, she should 'ask the Govern-
ment to place her upon that outdoor relief'
which is intended by the system of special
duties for the protection of special trades. I
do not believe the workmen of Coventry are
less able to fight the battle of competition than
are the workmen of Bradford or Birmingham
or Rochdale; and when the old cry of Pro-
tection is so thoroughly worn out in your
ancient city that it can no longer serve a local
political purpose, I suspect we shall hear no
more of it even from you. lam sorry to
-trouble lou with so long a reply. In future
I mist ask you to,forgive me if am silent.—
I am, respectfully yours, JOIDT BRIGHT.
Mr. Nathaniel Poole, 36, Swanswell-street,
Coventry."

CORRESPONDENCE.

We are not answerable for the opinions expressed by our

ELECTORAL REFORM.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

SlR,—More than twenty years ago, I think,
I made something like the following sugges-
tions in a provincial paper, in relation to the
franchise question :-
1. That borough representation be abolished,
and county representation on an assimilated
basis be substituted in its place.
2. That the aggregate of members elected
for the House of Commons be reduced to about
400.
3. That the number of members allowed to
each county be determined either by the
amount of general taxation levied in any
form on such county, or by the amount of_tax-
able income in such county.
4. That in accordance also with taxation or
taxable income, the population of each county
be divided into three sections, each section
after its own fashion, wither without hustings,
&0., with or AN ithout voting papers, and either
with Or without ballot, &e., electing its own
members.
5. That every man who pays taxes, direct
or indirect, i.e., every man of a certain age,
of sound mind, &c., should have a vote, and
that, in accordance with a fixed scale, payers
of large amounts of taxation should be allowed
extra votes, since, under such a mode of
representation, neither universal suffrage on
the one hand, nor a plurality of votes on the
other, would any longer appear objects of dis-
trust or fear, or, as now loom only in the future
as outward and visible signs of a coming and
palpable national injustice.
6. That the ;taxation, &o, both of coutties
and individuals always being known, the
number of members to be apportioned to each
county, and to each class of such county, as
well as the number of votes to be allowed to
each individual in such counties, be annually
published by the proper fiscal authorities.
7. That no one, unless possessed of a plu-
rality of votes, be allowed to vote for more
than one candidate, but that persons possessed
of a plurality of votes may either give all
their votes to one candidate, or divide them
between a number of candidates not greater
than the number of their votes.
8. That no candidate be allowed to receive
more than a proportional share of the aggre-
gate number of votes apportioned to the class
he seeks to represent, but that having secured
the voting papers, &0., of such proportional
share of class votes, or of the approximation
to such proportional share, he shall always be
considered duly elected as the patliamentary
representative of his special constituency.
9. That at the public requisition or declara-
tion of two-thirds of' such special constituency,
any member so elected be at once compelled to
vacate his seat, and that such special con-
stituency forthwith be empowered to elect at
will a more congenial representative in his
place—such member not having been elected
to a House of Representatives, as a represen-
tative of himself, but as a representative of
the special constituency alluded to.
10. That special honorary representatives of
the Army, Navy, Law, Church, and other im-
portant institutions or interests in the country,
be allowed seats in the House with the
privilege of speakine, but not of voting on any
measurt that come before them.
11. That the same privilege of speaking
but not of voting in the House be accorded
also with seats to a limited number of men of
mark in the country, selected either by the
Crown or by the House itself.
12. That cabinet ministers, and ex-cabinet
ministers, both prospectively and retrospec-
tively be always ex-officio perpetual members
of the House on similar terms, and that a like
distinction be awarded to representatives who
have held seats in the House for any given
number of years.
Hoping that the above propositions may
seem not altogether out of place during the
present recess whpn the s.lbject is in a great
measure under public consideration,—l am, &c.
London. W. A. RUSSELL.

articles.text:
SOLDIERS IN HARVESTING.

It will be recollected that at the end of last
August complaints were made through the
press, by the Council of the Warwickshire
Labourers' Union, and by other bodies of
agricultural labourers, that soldiers wore being
allowed to work at getting in the harvest for
many farmers in the midland counties who had
locked out their labourers, and would not
employ them on account of their being members
of the Labourers' Union. The matter was
brought under the notice of Mr. Cardwell, as
Secretary for War, calling the attention of the
Government to the injustice thus being perpe-
trated against the Union labourers, and giving
the names of several farmers, who, their
labourers being looked out or on strike, were
allowed the use of soldiers for the harvest
work,

The following communication was received
from the War Office on Tuesday :

War-office, Nov. 25, 1872.

Srn,—With reference t* my letter of the 9th of
September last, promising that the facts connected
with the recent employment of soldiers in gather-
ing in the harvest should be inquired into, I am
directed by Mr. Secretary Cardwell to acquaint
you that he finds that in the great majority of in-
stances neither strikes nor disputes between
farmers and their lahonrers existed, but that in a
few eases there were such disputes; and in answer
to his inquiries it appears, as was perhaps to be
expected, that the facts are somewhat differently
represented on the two sides; and therefore, it
may be matter of doubt whether the intention of
the Queen's Wgulations has been uniformly ob-
served. It is certainly not the intention of the
Queen's Regulations, nor the wish of her Majesty's
Government, that the employment of soldiers shall
be made use of to effect the result of such disputes.
The legitimate objects of that employment are the •
affording assistance in gathering in the harvest
for the benefit of the whole community, and the
permitting soldiers to turn to a profitable account
a portion of their time which would be otherwise
unoccupied. Care will be taken to prevent, in
future, the existence of any questions whether
these legitimate objects have been exceeded. The
harvest is over for this year, and the number of
soldiers employed in these few cases has been in-
considerable, and it does not appear to Mr. Card-
well that anything now remains to be done, except
to provide against the recurrence in future of any
such disputed cases. I am therefore directed to
inform you that the following Regulation will be
published as an addition to the existing Regula-
tions :—" Article 180 (Queen's Regulations), under
which general officers have hitherto been autho-
rized to allow the assistance of soldiers in gather-
ing in the harve3t, viz.: Such permissions will
not be granted in cases where strikes or disputes
between farmers and their labourers exist. All
Hitch cases should be reported to the Secretary of
State."—' am, Sir, your obedient servant,
J. C. VIVIAN.
, Mr. G. Shipton, Secretary of London Trades
Council.

afternoon on the body of a young man, whose
name is at present unknown. Afiehael Dono-
van deposed that on Sunday morning he saw a
box floating in the sea near the Brighton pier.
Ile got it on shore and sent for the police.
Inspector George Packha.m, of the Sussex con-
stabulary, said that when he opened: the box
at the dead-house. he found that it contained
the body of the deceased, who had been appa-
rently between 26 and 30 years of age. It
also contained a blue striped shirt, two guern-
seys, two pairs of trousers' a bed quilt, So.
Attached to .the box were two sacks, one of
which contained some coal, the other being
empty. Mr. J. R. Rogers, surgeon to the
Sussex police said that the deceased had only
been dead about two or three days. There
was a simple fracture of the left thigh, but
otherwise there was nothing to lead him to
express an opinion as to the cause of death.
After bearing further evidence the Coroner

About four o'clock on Tuesday morning two
constables, finding the front door of a tavern
in Duke-street, Adelphi,- known as the St.
Martins, open, entered the house and proceeded
upstairs to alarm the inmates. The landlord,
Mr. Alexander, his wife, and the barmaid,
were alarmed at hearing the footsteps on the
stairs, Mr. Alexander having especially been
warned against burglary or ineendiarism. He
at once seized a sword, and called to his wife
.to bring his pistols, and went out on the land-
ing. On seeing the dark figures on the stairs
he made a cut at the foremost one, and the
landlady was about to fire, when, owing to
the light of one of the lanterns carried by the
men, it was discovered that they were police-
men, and that there was no actual cause of
alarm, One of the officers had a narrow es-
cape, as the landlord, in cutting at him with
his weapon, took off soma of the buttons of his
coat.

LATEST INTELLIGENCE.

FRIDAY.

The Bank directors at their meeting yester-
day, after a long consultation, decided on
making a reduction of 1 per cent. in the official
minimum, making the amount now 6 per cent.
The inquiry ;for discount has been very
limited. Money is exceedingly abundant, and
the brokers work readily at from 51 to 6 per
cent.

Yesterday morning a considerable improve-
ment was reported in the state of the health of
both the Lord Chief Justice of Common Pleas
and of Lord Chief Justice Cockburn. All the
dangerous symptoms in both cases have totally
disappeared.
A telegram has just been received from the
Rev. Mr. Spurgeon, who is in the south of
France, stating that ho has been taken sud-
denly and seriously ill.
Lord Harris was buried in the family vault
at 'Throwley Church yesterday morning. The
coffin was followed by his son, the present
baronet; the Hon. Temple Harris, half bro-
ther ; and the tenantry and .labourers on the
estate. Colonel Kingscote attended as the re-
presentative of his Royal Highness the Prince
of Wales; and the Hon. Miss F. Stout r as
that of her Royal Highness the Princess. The
service was read by the vicar, the Rev. F. F.
Wallond, who was attended by the vicars of
Faversham, Boughton, and Selling.

The death was yesterday announced of
Lady Auckland, which took place at Wells,
Somerset, on the 25th inst. Her ladyship was
the daughter of Francis E. Hurt, Esq., of
Alderwasley, Derbyshire, and married, in
1825, the Right Rev. Robert John Eden, third.
Baron Auckland, successively Bishop of Sodor
and Man and of Bath and Wells, who died in
1870.

At Wednesday's meeting of the London
School Board, the resignation of Sir Thomas
Tilson was announced, on account of failing
health. A. deputation of managers of volun-
tary schools, having been introduced, pro-
tested against what they termed the extrava-
gant expenditure of the Board. Lord Lawrence
promised that due attention should be paid to
the representations which had been made, and
assured the deputation that the Board were
really endeavouring to supply efficient educa-
tion without subverting the establishments
which already exist.

terday the sum of £l,OOO was voted from the

the metropolitan district was 106,778, of whom

ceived out-door relief. Compared with the
corresponding weeks in 1871, 1870, and 1869,
these numbers show a decrease of 11,742,
30,635, and 35,668 respectively. The num-
ber of vagrants relieved was 779.

Liberal Association to take advantage of Mr.

December, for the purpose of expressing the
continued confidence of the Liberal party in
the present Administration.

nesday, announced at a meeting at Ilervie

night at Warrington. The hon. gentleman

people was loudly and emphatically expressed,

Common Pleas yesterday, Mr. Justice Brett

tion by Sedeant Parry when the court

men comprising platers, rivetters, &0,, en-
gaged at Messrs. Palmer's iron ship-building
yard, Jarrow, came out on strike. The men
refused to commence work during the -Winter
