in voting on the Bill, and that it was desirable
for other reasons that the Government should
have a majority in the Chamber. In this
sense the German Liberal organs continue to
demand a reform of their House of Lords.

A deputation from the Liverpool Land and
House Owners' Association had an interview
with Mr. Graves, M.P., and Mr. Ralhbone,
M.P., respecting local taxation, on Tuesday.
The deputation insisted on the injustice of
real property having to bear the whole of the
burden, and pointed out the necessity for an
alteration in the law. Mr. Graves and Mr.
Rathbone admitted the importance of the
subject, Old expressed the opinion that
Government, in the ensuing session, would
attempt to deal with it in a comprehensive
spirit.

Chart( r and Hardwick, the two men charged.
with the Pickering murders, have been com-
mitted for trial at the York assizes.

The first petition under the Ballot Act
against the return in a municipal election will
come from Birmingham. The petition alleges
impersonation, treating, undue infitienoe, and.
fictitious ballot papers. The majority was thrce
votes, by which a Conservative gained a viotoi y
over a Liberal.

There is not the slightest foundation in the
report published at the commencement of the
week of the death of Miss Eliza Cook, the
poetess, and the statement, as well as others
equally untrue, has been promptly contra-
dicted by the lady's medical adviser, who is
also a personal friend.

At the Liverpool Police Court on Wednet-
day the Liverpool Omnibus and Tramways
Company were fined ss. and costs for posting
advertisements on their omnibuses without the
consent of the corporation. It was stated that
some of the omnibuses were so lavishly pla-
carded that it was difficult to see their desti-
nation.

In the Court of Queen's Bench, on Wedner-
day, an action was tried in which Mr. Hard-
ing, accountant, recovered £650 damagcs
against Messrs. Baxendale, the well-known
carriers, for injuries inflicted upon two valu-
able pictures in their transit from London to
Paris. During the hearing the practice of
" bidding to keep up the prices" of paintings
which are ofThred for sale by auction elicited
an expression of disapprobation from Mr.
Justice Quain.

On Wednesday; Mr. Robert Evans, slice
manufacturer, of Cherry-street, Statrord, was
run down by a luggage train while crossing
the line at Rugeley station, and so much
injured that one of his legs had to be ampu-
tated. The train was going very slowly at
the time, but the unfortunate man, being
blind with one eye, did not voe its approach.
He is reported to be going on favourably. '

The ten men of St. Ives, who were blown
out to sea in two fishing boats, are now quite
given up for lost.

At the Marylebone Police-court, yesterday,
Susannah Long, aged 28, deseribed on the
charge-sheet as a milliner, living at No. 1,
Willing's-place, Church-place, Paddington,
was charged before Mr.. Mansfield with
,being,
a disorderly person and causing a crowd. to
assemble at Carlisle-street. Tao defendant
was wearing a. long black overcoat and black
trousers, and had a scarf round. her neck. Her
hair was cut short and parted in the centre,
Mr. Mansfield said it was very foolish cooduat
of the defendant, who would have to pay a
fine of 55., or in default to be imprisoned for
seven days. The fine was at once paid.

On Wednesday the remains of the late Sir
John Bowring were interred at Exeter. The
funeral was largely attended by the leading
men of the city and county. The Committee
of the British and Foreign Unitarian Assbeia-
tion have passed a vote of sympathy with Lady
Bowling and her family.

The Archbishop of Canterbury, speaking at
Broadstairs on Wednesday, remarked upon the
growing public sense of the importanee of
missionary work. At the same time, his
Grace regretted that the supply of persons
ready to go forth into foreign lands did not
appear to be adequate to the necessities of the
benighted heathen.

Sir Jams Hannon, the new Judge of the
Probate and Divorce Court, and Mr. Peter
Erie, Commissioner of Charities, 'were on
Wednesday sworn as members of thOT Privy
Connoil.

articles.title: TliE WEEK'S NEWS.
articles.text:
TliE WEEK'S NEWS.

Her Majesty the Queen arrived at Windsor
Castle shortly before nine o'clock on Saturday
morning from Balmoral, which had been
quitted on Friday afternoon. During the
absence of the Court great alterations and im-
provements, principally in regard to drainage,
have been made at the Royal residence, where,
however, the Queen will not nOw make a long
stay, intending to spend Christmas at
Osborne.

Arriving at the Berlin Schloss on Friday
afternoon, the Duke of "Edinburgh was received
by the Emperor Wilhelni at the entrance to
thellohenzoilern apartments. A private dinner
with the Emperor, and a visit to the Opera,
completed the day's work; and on Saturday
his Royal Highness, after a quiet time spent
"fn famine with his Imperial hosts, was present
at a grand dinner ia the Imperial Palace.

"Guy Fawkes" the young hippopotamus,
was visible to the select public in the Zoologi-
cal Gardens on Sunday. The young animal
is progressing favourably, and seems to
have a better chance of life than his prede-
oessors.

The Court of Bankruptcy having refused to
register a resolution of the creditors of Mr.
F. Strange for a composition of one shilling in
the pound, on a technical informality having
been raised, there will be another meeting of
creditors, at which the same proofs and proxies
may be used. At the same time this is not
to interfere with the proceedings in bank-
ruptcy up to adjudication, but not beyond.

Paul Julius Mal, who was acquitted last
week of the murder of Hermann Nagel, was
on Monday brought up at Bow-street, under
the Extradition Treaty, charged with having
'committed a forgery in Berlin. Sir Thomas
Henry committed him to take his trial in the
Prussian capital.

A box has been washed upon the shore at
the east end of Brighton containing the body
of a man—apparently a foreigner, about 30
years of age—and a sailor's clothing. Attached
to the box were two bags of coals, seemingly
employed to sink it, and, in the opinion of the
police surgeon, life had not been extinct more
than about forty-eight hours. There was a
fracture of one thigh, but no other mark of
violence.

Sunday being the fifth anniversary of the
execution of Allen, Larkin, and O'Brien, at
Manchester, for the murder of Constable Brett,
it was observed in the usual manner in Cork.
A memorial cross is erected at St. Joseph's
Cemetery to the memory of the " martyrs,"
and between three and four o'clock largo crowds
of people visited the place, where prayers for
,the dead were being recited. There was no
other demonstration.

In a pastoral read in all the Roman Catholio
churches of Dublin, Cardinal Cullen alluded to
the educational question, but with a milder
assertion of the claims of the Church than in
his previous address. His Eminence limited
himself to declaring in substance that, both in
primary and higher education, parents should
take care that their children were not exposed
to any influences dangerous to their faith, and
expressed a hope that in dealing next session
with the University question, the Legislature
would provide adequate protection for the
religious principles of Catholics.

In nearly all the Presbyterian churches in
Edinburgh, on Sunday last special reference
was made to the life and influence of John
KIIOXI in connection with the tercentenary
commemoration of his death.

Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Lowe received on
Saturday, at the Treasury, a deputation from
the Board of Works, who sbek the aid of
Government in freeing all the metropolitan
bridges from toll, by the continuance for ten
years longer of the coal and wine duties.
Colonel Hogg, who headed the deputation,
explained that it was intended to malts free
twelve bridges in all; and after some conver-
sation, the two Ministers promised that the
matter should be brought before the Cabinet,
and receive consideration.

Derry election resulted in the return of Mr.
Conservative, with 696 votes, and 174
over Lewis,;he Attorney-General. The only effect
of the Home Rule candidature was to secure
for Mr. Biggar 89,V0te3 and lose a Liberal seat.
When the error was discovered, a number of
the Home Rulers are said to have gone over to
Mr. Palles, but it was too late. The first trial
of the Ballot in Ireland was a perfect success
in the preservation both of secrecy and order.

telegram from Lille states that Mr. Cas-
per, the English merchant who has just been
tried there on a charge of defrauding the
French Government in connection with some
military contracts during the late NVar, has
been acquitted.

A locomotive engine, belonging to the Brecon
and Merthyr Railway Company, was being
driven along a branch of the line overhang-
ing the river Taff, when the driver, owing to
some cause unexplained, was unable to stop
the en gine, which rolled down the embank-
ment hato the river, flooded by the late rains.
The driver escaped unhurt.

Sergeant Bates, the bearer of the "Stars
and Stripes," received an ovation at Learning
ton on Monday. In an address of welcome to
the town, ho was assured that not only would
the American flag not be insulted, but that
"the heart of England beat warmly for her
children who have founded happy homes on
the iihorca wasljed,'by the Pacific, the Atlantic,
and the Arctic Oceans." The sergeant
acknowledged with much feeling the kindly
reception he had everywhere met with. A
tradesman of the town: also presented him
with a gold Maltese cross as a memento' of the
occasion. He expects to reach London to-day
(Saturday).

A gipsy hawker has been brought before the
Wandsworth Police Magistrate charged, under
the Vagrant Act, with having pretended to
tell fortunes. The proseoutrix was a domestic
servant, who left her situation on Friday night
last with 3 16s. in her possession. On the
gipsy undertaking to give her some informa-
tion respecting a young man, the girl handed
to the prisoner all the money she had, the
latter having promised to return with it at a
stated time. As she did not keep her word,
she was arrested, and when brought to the
police-station she remarked that "if there
were no fools there would be no.living." A
sentence of three months' imprisonment, with
hard. labour, was passed.

The inquiry into the death of a man named
Waine, who was kicked to death near Bishop
Auckland on the 16th instant, on Monday
ended in a verdict of wilful murder against
three men, who were committed for trial.

At the Guildhall Police-court, on Monday,
further evidence was taken in the case of a
woman named Fox, of Rolls-yard, Bermondsey,
who is charged with having committed perjury
in a trial at the October Session of the Central
Criminal Court, when George Thomas Condy,
a solicitor, and Henry Harvey, an accountant,
were convicted of a conspiracy to defraud.
The hearing was again adjourned, after an
intimation from Mr. Alderman Carter that
thus far the testimony for the prosecution was
not of a conclusive character.

Several charges of assaulting the police were
heard before the metropolitan magistrates on
Monday, and sentences were passed, varying
from a fine of 40s. to six weeks' imprisonment
with hard labour.

The British troops evacuated the island of
San Juan on Friday last week.

Lieutenant-General Guillaume has, at the
earnest solicitation of his colleagues, con-
sented provisionally to retain the portfolio of
the Belgian Minister at War.

The Maguire Fund amounts to £3,000, and
includes 25 guineas from the President of the
Board of Trade,

On Tuesday morning an accident occurred
to a passenger train on the Burton Branch of
the Midland Railway. The train which leaves
Burton shortly after eight o'clock and arrives
in Leicester at 9.20 was approaching Bardon-
hill Station, when an empty waggon-train
belonging to a stone quarry close by was
being shunted, and, before the driver could
get the waggons into the siding, the passenger
train dashed into the middle of the empty
waggons as they stood across the up and
down lines, cutting the waggon-train almost
in two. Several of the passengers were
severely shaken; one, named Beckwith, a
builder, was considerably bruised.

The American Commission under the Treaty
of Washington have rejected British claims to
the amount of 10,000,000 dols.

Prime Charles of Prussia, attended by a
number of Prussian officers, is about to go to
St. Petersburg to attend the fete of St. George,
on December Ist.

A. marriage is spoken of between the
Princess Thyra of Denmark with the Prince-
Royal of Hanover, son of the ex-King George.
The bride is the sister of the future Queen of
England and of the prospective Empress of
Russia.

The "Countess of Derwentwater" was
arrested on Monday atNewland's-grange farm,
near Shotley-bridge, for contempt of court in
relation to some proceedings in the Newcastle
County Court. She was conveyed to New-
castle and lodged in gaol.

The Kincardineshire farmers at a meeting
on Monday resolved to request Sir George
Balfour to come forward as the Liberal candi-
date for the county.

Mgr. Merode, says a Reuter's telegram, is
laid up from the effects of a fall front a stair-
case, and his illness is becoming serious.

A fire occurred late on Monday night at the
residence of Captain Bond, Nelson-terrace,
Trafalgar-road, East Greenwich. After tbe
flames were extinguished, Engineer Percival,
of the London brigade, discovered the body of
Mrs. Bond, aged 79, who had been burnt to
death.

An agrarian outrage is reported from Clare.
A gentleman, named Arthur Gethin Creagh,
was fired at near his own residence, Carreghan,
about Ox miles from Ennis, oa the road to
Tulle. Ho was slightly wounded. The
intending assassin made oil', and has not been
arrested up to the present time. It is believed
the blunderbuss burst in his hands and
wounded him slightly.

We learn that Lieutenant J. Graham
Smith, 57th Regiment (late Ist West India
Regiment), with was severely wounded in the
lath 'lndian raid. upon British Honduras, has
arrived home from Belize, his wound having
healed more
,rapialy than was at first expected-,
though the bullet has not yet been extracted.
We regret to say, however, that Lieutenant
Smith has been suffering from fever induced
by the physical weakness and consequent
shook to the nervous system caused by the
wound in the lung, and aggravated by the
mental anxiety of the three or four days which
elapsed between the attack on Orange Walk
and the arrival of the.. reinforcements from
Belize.

The trial of Father O'Keeffe's action for
•libel against the Cardinal has been postponed
to next term, owing to the serious illness of
Canon Ford.

It is stated that the German Federal
Government intend to convoke a special com-
mission to draw up a bill for levying a tax on
the transfer of securities.

A report has come from New Zealand which
would have excitedvery greatinterest amongst
the community if it had been credited. The
statement, which was published in the Auckland
papers, is to the following effect:—" Private
information of a most reliable and highly
influential kind has lately been received by a
gentleman in Tauranga, from relations at home,
that His Royal Highness and the Princess of
Wales intend to travel eastward, visiting the
various dependencies of the Empire in thiS
part of the globe, including Australia and New
Zealand."

In his Message President Grant will urge
that prompt legislative measures should be
taken in order to prevent the recurrence of
outrages committed on the frontier by the
Mexicans.

The death is announced of Mr. John Osborne
Q.C., County Court Judge of Circuit No. 5.
He oily received the appointment last year.
The circuit embraces part of Lancashire and
the West Riding of Yorkshire.

The London correspondent of the Scotsman
says there is a movement on foot among the
Roman Catholic nobility in this country and
on the Continent, for bringing about a gene-
ral agreement to abstain from giving enter-
tainments during the coming season, and
from participation in festivities, in considera-
tion of the present distressed state of the Church
and of its head.

A scheme is before the Ventnor Local Board
for establishing direct railway communication
between the Isle of Wight and the main land,
without change of carriages; By the scheme
it is proposed to construct a permanent sloping
way at Ryde and Southsett or Portsea Piers,
together with a tidal floating pier, to allow
for the rise and fall of tide, and secured tor
bad weather to form a medium to steam-
packets, in the centre of which deck a depressed
set of rails would receive the railway carriages
by the aid of a steam capstan. It is said that
the journey from London to Ventnor might be
accomplished in 31 hours, without any change
of carriages.

Dr. W. C. Bennett's "Songs for Sailors" will
be issued next Monday in two forms—a library
edition and a shilling people's edition, as the
author holds that a new work should be placed
at once within the reach of all classes.

Lord Harris died suddenly, we believe from
apoplexy?, at an early hour on Saturday morn-
ing at Belmont, his seat, near Faversham,
Kent.

Martha Howard, "a . little old woman,"
was brought to Worship-street accused of
aisaulting her husband, who is described as
being a little person also. In the first instance,
she pulled all their mutual bed-clothes from
him, and, on his remonstrance, smacked him
about the body with a piece of iron lath, and,
besides, intlieted a wound on his face. She
was ordered to find bail for good behaviour in
the sum of 40s.

Additional partioulars of the disaster to the
steamer Kinsale are reported. The Kinsale
was owned by the Clyde Shipping Company,
and traded between Glasgow, Cork, and Water-
ford. On the night of Monday week she left
Greenock on her usual passage to the Irish
ports named, and, having disoharged her carp
at Cork, sailed on her return trip to the Clyde.
As she was nearing the 'entrance to Waterford
Bar on Saturday morning, the shaft of her
engine broke, and it is beyond doubt that,
being helpless, she was driven ashore.
storm had been raging for some time, and she
seems to have been running into the bar for
shelter. The Kinsale soon became a total
wreck; and out of a crow of twenty only Ow
mate and two men were saved; while nine
passengers were also drowned, making a total
of twenty-six.

Queen Victoria has sent a donation of £lOO
for the relief of those who have suffered from
the late inundations in Rome.

The death is announcA of the Marquis of
Londonderry, who has been for some time
past in precarious health. The marquis had
long retired from society owinr, to his mental
malady. His lordship died on Monday even-
ing, the marchioness being present with him
at his dissolution. The relatives of his lord-
ship were not unprepared for his death, fur he
had. lingered several weeks without any hoPe
of recovery.

Mr. Robert Palmer, of Holme-park, near
Reading, who for 36 years represented Berk-
shire in the House of Commons in the Con-
servative interest, and for a long period was
chairman of the Barks quarter sessions, died
on Sunday night. The deceased gentleman,
who was much and widely esteemed, had
nearly attained his 80th year.

Sir John Lubbock has given permission to
his tenants on his estate at Luxted, Down°,
&e., Kent, to kill the rabbits
.on their farms,
on condition that they preserve the foxes, but
prohibits their shooting or trapping hares'ocr
winged game; and Earl Stanhope, Whose
estate adjoins, has extended a similar privilege
to his tenants.

A telegram has been received from the
Maharajah of Kuppoortalla, to the effect that
her Highness the Maharanee was safely de-
livered of a son and heir to the Musnud, 011
Monday. Her highness and the young Prince
are doing well. The birth of this Prince is
considered to be of some importance in Indian
politics, as settling the succession of the
principality.

With regard to the American Estimates
about to be presented to Congress, it is said
that they will be equal to those of the ladt
years. The Naval and Indian expenditures
will show a reduction, while sothers will be
increased.

At the commencement of the Roman Catholie
University in Stephen's-green, at Dublin ea
Monday, the Rector, Dr. Woodlock, in pre-
sence of Cardinal Cullen and several Bishops
and other dignitaries, delivered the inaugural
address. He treated almost exclusively of the
question of University eduoation, contending
that the Catholic University was not a
failure, but had done more than could have
been expected from the difficulties with which
it had to contend. Catholics, he said, asked
for equality in education, and would be con-
tent with nothing less.

The Bishop of Oxford has addressed the
archdeacons of his diocese to the effect that it
is intended to keep the 20th of December as a
day of united intercession to Almighty 'God on
behalf of missions. Its observance has the
approval of the archbishop of the.,provinee,
and his grace has authorized a service for the
diocese of Canterbury, which the bishop is
glad to recommend for use in the churches of
his diocese also. His lordship concludes hie
letter thus :—" Oar hope is that the Church
may bestir herself to a more united, and
therefore more effectual, supplication for the
extension in all the world of the kingdom 9f
our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ."

James Homer, the secretary to the WolYar"
hampton Gas 'Company, was charged 011
Monday with having on the 24th of April last
embezzled £174, the property of his employers.
The actual amount of his defalcations is said
to be £2,000. Prisoner returned to AVolver•
hampton on Saturday night, and vtiluntarSY
informed the police of his whereabouts. tie
was arrested at the shop of Mr. Booth, 00,0'
feotioner, Queen-street, Wolverhampton. oe
was remanded for a week, bail being refused.

The Supplementary Elections at Geneva br,
the General Council have resulted in the Radical
lists carrying the day almost entirely in t,lll°
three colleges. Inf. Turrettini, Wessel
Hartmann, and Revilliod are, however,a rope
the elected. Great agitation prevails
ecclesiastical circles, 14 Unitarian members 0
the Consistory having announced their intention
to resign on mount of the majority •of the
orthodox party.

German rationalism is credited with pro-
ducing a serious division in the Protestant
Consistory of Geneva. The schism arose from
an attempt' to bring into use a new catechism,
translated from the German, and " impreg-
'nated with Rationalist tendencies." This was
defeated, and fourteen members, nearly half
the Cousistory, have, in consequence, re.
signed.

In consequence of Count Lonyay having
himself informed the Hungarian Net that he
intends to cause a revision of all Government
contracts since 18G9, the hostility which
existed against his Cabinet in the Chamber is
appeased. The Diet has agreed to Deputy
Koromio's motion for a revision of the standing
orders of the House.

Legislative measures for the restoration of
American commerce to the condition in which
it was before the war will be recommended in
the Message of the President of the United
states. The renovation of the American navy
is urged in a report of the Secretary for that
Department. The estimated yield of the
American cotton crop is about an average,
being three and a half million bales.

Captain Tyler, inspector of railways, has re-
ported to the Board of Trade that the accident
at the Kelvedon Station of the Great Eastern
line, which occurred on the 19th of last month,
was not owing to any fault in the permanent
way, but to the weakness and failure of the
transverse spring of the engine, which
canoed it to oscillate and run off the rails.

Mr. George Hope, of Fentonbarns, has
declined the request to offer himself as a
second Liberal candidate for Forfarshire in
opposition to Sir James Ramsey.

An emigrant ship, the Royal Adelaide,
bound from London to Sydney, South
Australia, has been lost in West Bay, near
Weymouth, ineffectually, attempting to get
within the shelter of the Portland breakwater.
A considerable number of men, women, and
children were got off in safety by means of the
rocket apparatus, two, however, being drowned
in the attempt to land; but several of the
crew and passengers refused to leave the ship,
and perished in consequence.

Lord Granard presided at the first general
meeting of the Catholic Union of Ireland,
which was held in the side chapel of the
Cathedral, Marlborough-street, and, in his
opening address, said the union was essentially
Catholic, and non-political, its object being to
proclaim the sovereignty of Catholic interests
as paramount over every other, to sustain the
cause of the Pope, to watch legislation, and
promote Catholic education. Among the
speakers were Lord &Intim°ll, Sir John
Bradstreet, Mr. D'Aroy, M.P. Mr. Edward
Maguire, Mr. P. J. Smyth, Mr. Red-
mond, M.P., Mr. Cogan, IM.P., and Captain
Power Lalor.

Canon Lightfoot delivered the second of his
lectures to young men on Tuesday night, in
St. Paul's. The subject was Christian Life
in the Second and Third Centuries."

Writs for filling the vacancies in the re-
presentation of Kinoardinshire and Forfarshirc
will be issued on Monday next.

The nomination of candidates for the re-
presentation of Cork will take place on Mon-
day next, and the polling has been fixed for
Friday, December 6th.

On Tuesday the first annual meeting of the
National Union for Improving the Education
of Women was held at the rooms of the Society
of Arts. Lord Lyttelton presided, an 4
Amongst the speakers were Mr. C. S. Roun-
del', Mr. W. D. Christie, Canon Barry, Miss
Emily Davies, and the Rev. W. Arthur.

An inquiry has been held respecting the
death of a Welsh lady named Jones, the wife
of a landowner, who commuted suicide im-
mediately after rising from the dinner table
by leaping from a window in the Hove-villas,
Brighton, and was taken up dead. A verdict
of "Temporary insanity" was returned.

Another Cabinet Council was held at the
official residence of the Prime Minister on
Tuesday.

The Gazette contains an official intimation
that the Queen has appointed the Ron. and
Rev. F. B. C. Byng, Vicar of St. Peter's,
South Nensington, and honorary Chaplain to
her Majesty, to be one of the Chaplains in
Ordinary to the Queen, in the roam of the
Very Rev. B. M. Cowie, 8.D., Dean of Man-
chester; and has appointed the Rev. J. St.
John Blunt, M.A.., Vicar of Old Windsor,
Berkshire, and Chaplain to the Chapel,
Windsor, to be an honorary Chaplain to her
Majesty.

The meeting of the British Association at
Bradford has been fixed for Sept. 17, 1873.
The enbsoriptions already received to the
guarantee fund amount to £1,57ö.

Twenty-eight men in the employ of the
Dublin and Belfast Junction Railway Company
have been summoned before the Dundalk
magistrates for leaving their work without
notice, in consequence of one of their number
having been dismissed. A nominal penalty
was inflicted, and the men will return to
work.

A correspondent writes :—" The question of
admission of women to medical decrees in
Edinburgh University has been rather unex-
pectedly solved, at least for the present. Miss
Jex Blake, a foremost champion of the move-
ment, has actually been plucked in her
examinations, and sent back to complete her
scientific studies."

For five hours on Saturday the Lord Mayor
was engaged in hearing the adjourned cases
against persons captured in the raid on the
City betting clubs on the 15th ultimo. The
prosecution was abandoned as regards the
men, eleven in number, who were found at the
Swan public-house, along with Bacon and Lee,
sentenced to heavy fines on Saturday the 16tli
ultimo; nor was the case pressed against four
other persons taken into custody at the Ex-
change Club. Evidence was led to show that
Edward Ray, whom the prosecution consented
to try on a separate charge, had been concerned
in unlawful betting operations at the club;
and the Lord Mayor found him guilty. Two
other persons connected with the Exchange
were fined, and the rest were liberated on
their own resognisanoes, the case standing
over for three months, pending appeal in the
affair of Ray.

Notioe is given by the Metropolitan Railway
Company of the intention of the directors to I
apply to Parliament next Session for permis-
sion to abandon that portion of the under-
taking from Aldgate to Trinity-square,
Whitochapel. A vigorous opposition to the
application will be given by the inhabitants
of the East-end, who complain that they have
fewer facilities for railway travelling than the
residents of any other part of the metropolis.
The Liverpool Daily POBl publishes a letter
from Mr. T. Hughes, M.P., in reply to an in-
vitation from Liberal working men to become
a candidate for Liverpool at the next election.
Mr. Hughes, while he expresses himself flat-
tered with the invitation, does not at once
accept, but asks his correspondents to let the
matter stand, as there is not much prospect of
a general election until next autumn and no
one can yet tell on what issue the election may
turn.

No case of rinderpest having been reported
for four weeks, the infected districts of York-
shire are now declared free.

A report has been received of the wreck, on
the coast of Waterford, of the Glasgow, Cork,
and Waterford steamer Kinsale. The captain
and nine men were drowned.

Extensive arrangements are being made by
the Government of Ontario for promoting
emigration' to that province. Mr. Horrocks
has been appointed Chief Commissioner for
England and Wales, and Colonel Dennison,
Special Commissioner for Great Britain. They
sailed for England on Monday. Commissioners
have also been appointed for Scotland, Ireland,
Germany, and Alsace. They are instructed
to endeavour to attract principally rural im-
migrants.

The Advanced Liberal Association of Gates-
head have invited Mr. Tennant, the general
manager of the North Eastern Railway Com-
pany, to contest the borough when a vacancy
may occur.

On Monday night Mr. Baines, M.P., and
Mr. Alderman Carter, M.P„ addressed a large
meeting of Liberals at Leeds. Mr. Baines
highly praised the foreign policy of the Go-
vernment. Agreeing that the Treaty of Com-
merce with France was only an approximation
to free trade, he nevertheless accepted it as
better than nothing. The Ballot Act he held
was not to be judged by accidental elections,
and it had certainly been worth lighting for.
He was in favour of amending the 25th clause
of the -Education Act, if it could be done in
such a way as not to violate the oonsoientious
feelings of poor parents. The Licensing Act
was valuable as far as it went, but he thought
there were still too many public-houses.

Tens of thousands of acres of land in Somer-
set, along the valleys Parrett, Yee, and Tone,
are now flooded. The bank of the Parrett,
which recently gave way at Aller Moor, and
thus 'relieved Laugport from the flood, haS
been repaired, and the town is again deluged.
The lower parts of scores of houses are under
water, and the inmates have to take refuge in
the upper rooms. Miles of roadway are
covered with water, and drivers have to ,guide
their horses between the willow trees which
line the track. In some cases the water reaches
to the horses' backs.

The Bengal indigo crop this year is dezcrihe
as enormous.

The skiff race for £lOO between Janice
Lally and John Bright, hoth Newcastle men,
front the High Level Bridge to the Scotswood
Suspension Bridge on the Tyne. on Monday,
was won by Lally, who finished a length
a-head, after a well-contested and exciting
race.

A. telegram from Rome says :—" Signori
Pardoni, Vivaldi, Romanelli, Bonivard, and
Valpozzo, leaders of the Radical movement
in favour of universal suffrage, who were to
have taken part in the prohibited meeting in
the Colosseum, were arrested on Sunday night,
and imprisoned in the Casa Nuova. They are
to be indicted for high treason. A. ease P
Orsini bombs had been captured at the Leg-
horn Railway Station on Sunday directed to
Rome."

It is stated that Mr. Gladstone will deliver
the prizes at the Liverpool College on the 21st
December.

In anticipation of the American Budget, it
is stated, with an appearance of probability,
that the estimates to be presented to Congres
will not be below those of late years. By
"internal revenue reform," of which so much
capital was tried to be made on the sth of No-
vember, the President will declare in his Ales-
sage that he understands it to mean that
honesty and efficiency, and not political
opinions, are qualifications for office.

In consequence of the heavy rain, the
Severn and the Tem are overflowing their
banks. Seed sowing is still prevented by the
weather. .

A new journal, entitled La Resurrection,
advocating a Republic the reverse of Conser-
vative, was published in Paris at the end of
last week; but was suppressed by tho autho-
rities.

A Bill for the definitive establishment of ft
general coinage for GermrnT is to be laid be-
fore the Reichstag next session.

Ozenne, who had so much to do with
the negotiation of the modified French Com-
mercial Treaty, will represent France on the
Commission charged to settle the points left
undetermined.

There is no foundation for the report that
Mr. Mundella is to be opposed at Sheffield at
the next general eleotion by a Conservative
working man.

A number of new offioes for the transmission
of postal telegrams have been or are about to
be opened in the vicinity of several important
towns. For the future the postage on letters
addressed to Constantinople, and forwarded
by the route of Belgium and Germany, will
be reduced to sd. the half-ounce. Letters
sent unpaid or insufficiently paid will be
liable to an extra charge on delivery.

A public meeting was held on Monday
night in the Cutlers Hall, Sheffield, under the
auspices of the Land Tenure Reform Associa-
tion. There was a fairly numerous attend-
ance. Speeches were made denunciatory of
the present mode of tenure and taxation of
land, and resolutions were passed declaring
such modes to be injurious, and contrary to the
will of the people.

As a young man named Herbert Alger,
residing in Took's-court, Cursitor-street, was
passing Futlwood's-rents, Holborn, on his way
home about three o'clock on Monday morn-
ing, a man who was standing at the corner
with Several others asked him for a pipe of
tobacco. This request not being complied
with, the whole gang rushed upon the unfor-
tunate man and assaulted him with the utmost
brutality, inflicting, amongst other injuries,
two serious stabs, one in the thigh and the
other across the wrist, nearly severing the
hand from the arm. The unfortunate young
man managed to get holm, when he fainted
frotn loss of blood, and, medical aid being
called in, he was at once removed to the
hospital.

An application was made on Wednesday to
the Court of Queen's Bench for a rule nisi
calling upon the Incorporated Law Society to
show cause why they should not be directed to
examine a Mr. Clements touching his fitness
and capacity to be admitted to the roll of
attorneys. A singular feature of the case was
that the applicant, unknown to himself, and
without his consent, was represented at last
Easter Term examination by some other per-
son; so that to use the words of Mr. Justice
Blaokburn, be had already passed it by deputy.
It was suggested, however, that the real
ground of objection on the part of the society
was the fact of Mr. Clements having been for-
merly engaged in bueiness. The Court
'granted a rulo.

The Rev. joliu Biggin' s one of the junior
curates of St. Mary Magriatene, Taunton, has,
we hear, seceded to the Church of Rome. Ile
has been received into that oorntriuuion at St.
Mary's Church, Torquay.

. .
France is experienoing the predicted effect
of her heavy taxation. During the nine
months of the official year for which . returns
havubeen made there is a deficit in the yield,
as compared with the estimate, of over
£5,000,000, two-thirds of the. falling-off being
in the indirect taxes.

An important application was made to Vine-
Chancellor Malins on Monday to remove the
names of Lord Claude Hamilton, Mr. Hope,
and Mr. Graham from the list of Contributories
to the estate of the La Mancha Irrigation and
Canal Company, which is in liquidation. As
directors of the company, the names had been
placed in the list as liable for 100 shares, but
they in fact held only one each, and as it ap.
peared by a resolution of the company they
were not required to hold more, although the
minimum qualification "for future directors'
was 100 shares, Sir. R Malins ordered the mo-
tion to stand over till the first day of Hilary
Term. in the belief that there was a moral
obligation to the creditors of the company, and
one of which gentlemen in the position of the
applicants would not seek to rid themselves on
a technical ground. Later in the day Mr.
Higgins, on behalf of Mr. Trope, repudiated
any idea of relying on a more technical objec-
tion.

In reference to the murder of the old road-
mender, James Boon, killed while at his work
at Olney on Thursday, the murderer, David
Sharpe, has made a statement admitting his
guilt. He stands committed tor trial.

By an explosion of fire-darap at Walsall,
two men have been seriously and one slightly
injured at Highbridge Colliery, Pe'sal), near
the mine where the other recent calamity
occurred.

Lord Chief Justice Cockburn, in the Court
of Queen's Bench, has announced the date for
trial of the great ease of the Crown vorbus
Castro—in other words, the prosecution of the
Claimant for perjury. To take the case
in the present term was out of the question;
Hilary Term would not suffice, because, by
taking it then the Spring Circuits would b•
left unprovided for; and the only course
possible under the circumstances was to post-
pone the trial until Easter Term —on the
fifth day of which it should be oommenced, to
be continued to the end.

Japanese creditors ranked for two-thirds,
in the claim of £60,000 in all, against the
"Joint Stook National Agency Company,"
with regard to which a petition was presented
to Vice-Chancellor Matins, praying for the
continuance of voluntary liquidation. The
company was only a year old • it was brought
down by the failure of idessrs. Bowles
Brothers, the American bankers; and the
report of the assets were so favourable as to
make the 'Plea-Chancellor express his pleasure
at hearing that tha J.ipanese creditors would
be paid in full--idding a hope that they
would be, "for th,, honour of the British

nation."

At the Westminster Polioe-aourt, on Tues-
day, a respectably-dressed man named Wm .
Brown was convicted of assaulting two police-
men in the execution of their duty. He was
sentenced to three months' imprisonment with
hard labour, but later in the day this was
commuted to a penalty of £l3.

Two assaults upon tramway conductors were
heard on Tuesday at the Thames Edice-aourt.
Fines amounting to 20s. and 258. respectively
were inflicted.

Monday being the last day of Michaelmas
Term, the Chancery Courts adjourned for a
short vacation. The sittings after Term begin
on Monday next, and last until the 23rd Dee.

At the instance of the parochial authorities
Several persons were brought before the magis-
trate at Marlborough-street Police.court. on
Monday, charged with keeping distirclorly
houses, Mr. Newton committed the defeni-
ants for trial, but accepted. bail for their ap-
pearanee.

A bill is to be promoted in Parliament next
Session to enable a tramway to be constructed
along the Victoria-road and Grove-street,
South Hackney. it is promoted by art inde-
pendent company, who seek powers to effect a.
junction with the tramways already in exis-
tence iu the neighbourhood and obtain running
powers over them.

On Monday night, as the Claimant to the
Tiehborne estates was about leaving Euston-
square Station for Glasgow, for the purpose of
delivering a lecture at that place, he was
accosted by a gentleman who delivered to him
a message to the ell'ect that Lady Doughty
was dying, and that if he wished to see her
and take her depositions, he must attend upon
her at once. In consequence of this, the
Claimant left the station immediately, giving
his agent directions to proceed to Glasgow ana
postpone the meeting which had been an-
nounced for the next evening,

The demand everywhere of the artisans employed in

deemed advisable by the Labour Representation League

and friends favourable to the cause of Labour representa-

The proposed object :of the Conference is to devise a
plan of united action for the purpose of ens uring the
return to the next Parliament of some IlleMbers belonging
to the ranks of Labour.
This question has assumed a much greater importance

serious attention of the working classes to the necessity

franchise in order to secure an entrance for men of their

SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 30, 1872.

THE WESTMINSTER WORKING. MEN'S

LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.

Mn. GLADSTONE, it must be acknowledged,
has done a great deal to avoid his Administra-
tion from sinking in repute. In its original
formation, he strenuously exerted himself to
infuse into it a strong tincture of indubitable
thoroughness, and, after great pains, was re-
warded with success. In this respect, how-
ever, he was thwarted by the course of events
as they affect individual men in this world.
JonN BRIGHT, indeed, v as not the only member
of the Cabinet, whose name and career had been
identified with the general cause of political
progress: there are in it, as it is now from
day to day meeting, several men who, though
not of ability and experience equal to his, bad,
up to the time of their taking office, held and
kept the reputation of being men of the people,
almost as decidedly, if not as prominently, as

he. In one of these, however, the expectations
of such among us as were ever sanguine in
the matter, have been cruelly disappointed,
and this experience tends to carry us back,
with respect to others also, to the old conclu-
sion that a Radical in opposition is very apt
to become a renegade in office.
While saying these things, we are far from
forgetting the great public services which have
been rendered by the Patatu MINISTER since
he received the quEEN's commands to form a
Ministry. Should he do nothing more he will
have achieved for himself a bright page in
British history. In this work-day world,
however, the existing generation is apt to lose
sight of both past and future in the exigencies
of the present. We aspire, in the words of
the American sergeant marching across the
island, to be "a growing country, I tell you.".
Even Mr. GLA.DSTONE, therefore, has been un-
able to escape the insinuation, that even he,
with all his unquestioned services and un-
doubted merits, is, after all, the head of "
weak Whig Government." Little as lie may
relish the description, he will make no objec-
tion to the bestowment of an increase of
strength ; and, for our part, we sincerely, and
even earnestly, wish ho may obtain it. But,
in order to this, he will find it necessary, we
feel certain, to look to the ways of his official
household. For what has been already wit-
nessed? We have heard it admitted on the
one hand, that he would not have been in
power, and consequently would not have done
the deeds that give lustre to his fame, but for
the support at the polling-booths given him
by the Protestant Nonconformists of the
United Kingdom. On the other hand. it is
affirmed, and with most evident truth, that
the first use of this power in a matter consi-
dered by those Protestant Nonconformists of
vital importance, was made directly against
them, and in favour of a party opposed to
them, and, until thus propitiated, to the Mi-
nistry themselves.
Now, seriously, what encouragement is thus
held out to other sections of the community
to throw their weight with the same decision
as these deluded Dissenters into the
scale? Nevertheless we are willing
for the experiment to be tried, only we
earnestly recommend the taking of such
guarantees as there could be no question about, '
should implied contracts not be fulfilled to
the satisfaction of both parties. Perhaps, then,
the formation and launch of the 'Westminster
Working Men's Liberal Association may be
looked upon as the first stop towards
another experiment made with a view to
see whether the GI„IDSTONE Govern-
ment may be newly strengthened with-
out disappointment to the reasonable expecta-
tions. of a proportionate return to those who
furnish the moans of fortification. This move
on the part of the working men of Westmin-
ster possesses a peculiar interest for observers.
it stands in undisguised opposition to a pre-
viously existing body calling itself Conserva-
tive. We will not assume to know precisely
how much the latter is a name, and how
little a thing. The best solution of that ques-
tion will be the practical one. Wo all remem-
ber the Will o' the Wisp, by which, during a
thick mist in the political atmosphere, we were
apt to have been led astray, and perhaps
bogged. Loading Tories were really going to
take us under their special patronage; and we
wore called upon to open our foolish mouths,
and shut our eyes, and see what these new
benefactors would send us. It all came to
nothing, just because we kept our mouths
close shut, and our eyes wide open.

If, indeed, a number of the working men
are Conservatives it is natural that they should
loan on, and look to their own party. What,
however, can those of us do who hold Liberal
prinoiples, but look to the Liberal party and
its c)iiefs for what wo want, not as a class of
the community (which we repudiate) but as
nine-tenths of the whole community itself?
Well, then, the natural outcome of this
pitting of two bodies of the same kind, though
of different principles, one against the other,
will be, not simply to show which of the two
is the stronger and the more real, but, most of
all, for practical purposes, which of the two
can, at the next election, control the choice
of candidates to represent the city of

Westminster. If the Liberal working men
succeed in effecting the return of two Liberals,
Mr. GLADSTONE will understand the hint. And
if, as is nearly certain, the example thus set
in the immediate precints of Parliament be
followed the whole kingdom over, the Liberal
leader and all his followers will see the full
extent of their obligations to those who now,
politically as well as physically, constitute the
thew and sinew of the nation; and will, we
still venture to hope, see the sound wisdom,
no less than the common honesty of making
a due acknowledgement.

articles.title: TEM CRISIS IN FIUNCE.
articles.text:
TEM CRISIS IN FIUNCE.

AFFAIRS in France are critical indeed. At
the moment when we write it would be rash
, to predict how the crisis will issue, favourably
,or adversely. The probability, however,
leans, we are sorry to say, in a direction
adapted to excite pain and apprehension. No
moderation, in fact, appears to be expected
from the leaders of the majority in the National
Assembly, whatever suaveness of language
may be found in the report made by the
majority of the Committee to which the ques-
tion concerning the PRESIDENT of the REPUB-
LIC'S Message. A rupture, therefore, between
M. TIIIERS and the Assembly seems imminent ;
and should that ensue, the consequences to
the country may be fearful, unless the
" Radical" party should exhibit a power of
self-restraint hardly to he expected from
Frenchmen under such circumstances. One
country of Europe is immediately and inti-
mately concerned in the up-shot; but in point
of political progress or retrogression the matter
affects, more or less, every State and nation
besides. We therefore advise the working
men of Great Britain to watch every point
and turn in this momentous debate, not merely
with interest, but with close attention, and
with an application to themselves and their
prospects of everything in it that has a bear-
ing (and what has not, more or loss?) on their
own welfare, and the ways and means by
which it were wise and well to seek for the
full accomplishment of their just wishes.
The grand debate on which everything turns
was to begin on Thursday. Of this, at pre-
sent, we have no information, There is hope,
however, in the fact that it was postponed till
that day. Two reports are for consideration ;
that of the nine members of the Committee
who are Right or Right Centre men, that of
the six remaining members who are Left or
Left Centre men. The former, presented by
M. BATBIE, MI enemy to M. TIIIERS, recom-
mends simply the nomination of a committee
to prepare a Bill on Ministerial Responsi-
bility; the latter is described as adding to
Ministerial Responsibility measures (approved
by M. TmEns) for securing the proper work-
ing of a Republican Government.
Ono vote has been already taken. The
question was whether the report read by M.
BATBIE on Tuesday should be discussed at
once, or not till Thursday. The Right
clamoured for its instant consideration; the
Ministers and the Left advocated postpone-
ment, and postponement was carried by 356
against 332. A majority so narrow must
not be magnified into undue importance; it is
a majority, and that is all. If, it is said in
Paris and at Versailles, M. TRIERS can secure
as many votes on the discussion now pending,
the result will be a triumph for him. We
earnestly hope that whatever may be the effect
of the division, it will tend to the preserva-
tion of public order. But in an Assembly of
Frenchmen so nearly divided, we cannot look
with confidence for that calmness on either
side which, under such circumstances, ought
to be the characteristic of both. To do more
justice, indeed, the report presented by M.
BATBIE refers to the " Radicals " in terms
which would be a severe test to the equanimity
of the most stolid nation, let alone the most
vivacious race in the civilised world.

If ever the Committee appointed at the
instance of M. KERDREL was sincerely
designed, which must at least be doubted,
to smooth the way to reconciled feeling and
concerted action between the PRESIDENT of
the REIT-nue and the Right or " Rural"
party, now, at any rate, the breach yawns
wider and deeper than before. Notwithstand-
ing that use of contrivance which is seeond
nature with 14,_TurEns, ho looked up, to a

certain point, as though ho relied upon the
pretended desire of the Monarchist factions to
work with him, and frankly reciprocated it.
Much of what is reported as having occurred
between, him and the Committee wears this
semblance; and, of course, he would be
actuated, by a solicitude real enough, to in-
duce them, if possible, to come to a resolution
on tho basis of which he might carry on
his Government with as much harmony as is
practicable in the face of a declared Opposition.
And indeed, he could not have mustered the
large minority he did on Tuesday, unless
many of the more reasonable on the Right
(namely, the Right Centre) had been impressed
with a sense of the duty of shrinking from
extremes.

The votes of these gentlemen in association
with the Left and Loft Centre, must further
be construed with a proper reference to filo
explanations given before the Committee by M.
TITTERS as to the measures which ho holds
! necessary in fulfilment of his heavy under-
taking. These are, a prolongation of the
PRESIDENT'S powers, the appointment of a
Vice-President to provide for a certain
emergency, the clearer determination of the
relations betwixt PRESIDENT and Assembly.
To Ministerial responsibility, he would agree,
if coupled with these conditions; and, on
similar terms, the votes of the whole Left,
perhaps, would go in the like direction. All
then comes back to the standing point—does
Ti!. TITTERS, or does ho not, possess the con-
fidence of the Assembly ? It remains to be
seen, first, whether his explanation of what
will be to him an affirmative reply, will
dispose and decide a clear majority of the
Assembly to vote that way; and, secondly,
if the two-thirds of the Committee gain
the support of two-thirds of the Assembly,
what precise form and aspect they may
choose to give to their success. The
Report is in words complimentary enough to
M. TITTERS ; but, since it ignores altogether the
measures which he considers indispensable, the
personal compliments are only more certain
signs of the political aversion. The existing
Government of France has not the at-
tributes of a genuine Republic though
it has the name ; and, if the KER-
DREL Committee should have their way
(which we predict they never will), it
would be quite as far from being a Constitu-
tional Monarchy, whatever names or appear-
ances might be given to:it. Let our ktruggling
and suffering neighbours have a Republic or a
Constitutional Monarchy, whichever may
please them best; but let us all hope and pray
that the name and the thing will, in either
case, honestly agree. Theoretically M.
limns has no power to dissolve the Assem-
bly; practically the Assembly has not the
means of making its temporary dominion a
permanent sovereignty. Opinion must rule ;
and while opinion abroad will be impartial
in its award, opinion at home will not, beyond
a certain point, refrain either the utterance of
its voice, or the exercise of its action.

articles.title: CHURCH IN DANGER.
articles.text:
THE CHURCH IN DANGER.

IF the Church is really in danger, there is
but one way of saving it. Of course, it may
be defended by individuals and by societies.
An honest zeal may be displayed on its behalf,
as there are many honest persons who wish it
to be maintained as an institution exoellent in
its design, its working, and its object. Or it
may be defended by such persons as the Rev.
J. J. MANLEY, 'whose untruths we last week
exposed, and who no doubt regard everything
fair in controversy as in love, and therefore
invent facts and circulate slanders, believing
that the end sanctifies the means.

Without professing any kind of affection for
the Establishei Church, we feel it a duty to
assure its friends that such arts in its defeneo
can only hurry its downfall. The Church
gradually lost its inthtenco by not performing
its duties to the nation. It was full of a spirit
of controversy—could persecute on occasion,
could oppress honest consciences ; but it could
not performin a spirit of humanity and zeal
its duties to the suffering poor. And, above
all things, it could not resist the wrong-doer
if power and privilege were on his side. For
these things the Church lost its inhuman, and
if these continue the Church must continue tu

10

still urther lose it, until, rotten-ripe, it falls
of itself, without a friend beyond those who
have a corrupt interest in its existence. High
Churoh and Low Church zeal, whildt rending
it internally from roof to base, beget no
warmth in the minds of the outside masses,
who become daily more disgusted with men
who shirk their higher duties that they may
engage in low, discreditable brawls.
The one only way to save the Church is to
make it of use in the world,—for its clergy to
try and understand what the requirements of
society in its present condition are, and to
minister to these requirements in an honest,
active, and manly spirit. If the Church prove
its usefulness by its action it may be saved,
but unfortunately those who show themselves
most fit for this great work are least encou-
raged by the men who hold authority within
it, or by those who within or without distri-
bute its patronage. It would not be difficult
to point to instances where zeal for the im-
provement of the people in a liberal and manly
way was a bar to promotion. The case of the
late Professor MAURICE is a notable one in
point. His love for the people, and his gene-
rous and wise efforts on their behalf', were
evidently regarded as dangerous heresies not
to be encouraged, and though his elevation to
the bench would have done more to popularise
the Church than a dozen crusades against
candles, costumes, or papal attitudinising, he
was allowed to wear his life out without any
kind of suitable recognition.
The Rector of Bethnal Green, the Rev.
SEPTIAIUS HANSARD, is another case in point.
It is impossible to take note of his useful
activity and broadly liberal proceedings,
without asking ourselves why, instead of
being acknowledged for his usefulness, he is
passed over by those above him, and made a
butt for the pious but poisoned arrows of
every bigot, lay and clerical, to whose narrow-
ness of heart and mind his wider and more
generous efforts are a reproach. The distribu-
tion of prizes last week by the Lona) MAYOR
at his schools in Bethnal Green was a sight
not to be forgotten. Young working men and
children of the very humblest people, by his
help and encouragement had worked hard for
their prizes and won them, and received them
from the hands of the LORD M.troa without a
syllable of cant as to their stations in life, or
as those whom Providence had placed above
them, but with many syllables of sound and
manly advice as to their duties in life as
men and women, and as to the ennobling
influence of culture on the heart and con-
science.

If in every parish church in England such a
sight could be seen as was witnessed on the
21st of the present month at Bethnal Green,
the Church of England could not be said to be
in any great danger. Those who belonged to
it would love it and defend it for the good
received by them from it, while those outside
Its communion would respect and spare it for
its wise labours, on behalf of education and
progress, and for its efforts in the promotion
of a Christian and wise liberality. But as
we have already said, to do these things is not
to win favour in the Church, but rather to
earn suspicion and incur neglect. If popular
services and. sermons hare to be got up in St.
i'aults or elsewhere, such men as the Rector of
Bethnal Green are not the persons invited
to address the people, something liberal
might slip out, and such a thing is at all
times and under all circumstances most un-
fleeirable to those in authority. Upon the
whole the Church does not encourage her

liberal, manly, hard-working ministers, and
does not, as a natural consequence, do such
work as gives her a claini on the confidence
and respect of the country. And, therefore,
the " Church" really is "in danger."

articles.title: UNDER TIIE LIME-LIGHT.
articles.text:
UNDER TIIE LIME-LIGHT.

Tun Telegraph, a few days since, gave an
account of a costermonger's tea party, at which
there was much hearty eating of bread and
butter, described with a good deal of pleasant
unpleasantness—if such a form of speech be at
all allowable; pleasant by the graphic skill of
the description, as well as by the intention
and spirit of the whole thing; unpleasant to
painfulness by the assurance it gives of the
ignorance, debasement, And squalor it reveals

as part and parcel of our social life as a
nation. These poor people, wonderfully good
and kind, everything considered, are passed by
unnoticed in our streets- as vendors of cheap
wares; but gathered together on some great
occasion they constitute a foul blot on our
social system, which it would take much
preaching in church and chapel to exouse, and
which nothing but habit could make endur-
able to people who admit that Christian duty
should be realised in life, and that the bene-
volence of Christian thought should be con-
stantly operative for the alleviation of human
misery.

What we have to thank the writer in the
Telegraph for, however, is not his well-
written paragraphs, or the picturesque cha-
racter of his style, so much as the Asmodcan
glimpse ho gives us into the homes of our
poor. Cow-cross is not far from the residences
of our aristocratic and trading millionaires ;
yet Tahiti or Fiji, where the inhabitants can ,
indolently and comfortably sun themselves
under the loaded branches of their bread-fruit
trees, receive far more thought and assistance
than the poor dingy commonplace coster-
monger. There is a fashion in philanthropy,
and, as in many other fashions, the prefer-
ence is given to the foreign article. A nice
black, whose lips are sufficiently thick, whose
head is woolly, and wltose nose is flattene d
to the proper level, is a much more interest-
ing subject than a grimy-skinned man who
sells fish or vegetables about the streets of
London; whilst the heithenism of the savage
is infinitely more powerful to excite the sym-
pathy of sensitive West-end and pious people,
than the heathenism of those who „though
living in the midst of our churches and chapels,
never darken their doors, because, neither by
knowledge nor sympathy, do they care about
what is passing within them.
The following deScription of the effect of
the limo-light on the dwellings of these poor
People in the neighbourhood of Cow-cross is
painfully interesting. Human life, under all
its aspects, is interesting ; and, if the same
light which made the interiors of the Cow-
cross habitations visible could be applied to
all London, it is certain a Bight might be
revealed which would move the most callous
heart to indignation and pity. The writer
says :

It was startling to see the fashion in which the
inexorable lime-light ripped away the dense alley
mist that clung like a sable cloak about these
horrible habitations, and exposed them. You could
see through the uneurtained windows sheer into
scores of rooms, plainly as you can into a dingy
corner when a bull's-eyo light is flashed upon the
spot; the walls bare and smoke-begrinacd, the
floor naked, except for the sack or strip of old
carpet before the fonderless fireplace round about
which the squalid family huddled. You could see,
as plainly as though you were within three yards
of them, what were the rags they wore, and how
insufficiedt they were to cover the poor little
bodies of the children. You could make out, too,
quite distinctly, what a dreadful contrivance a
Cow-cross-alley bedstead is in many eases, and
picture to your mind what a terrible hardship you
would find it to have to lie on su eh a heap of raga
and under such a coverlet. Ho w cold it must be
—taking into account the broken ceiling and the
broken windows—in the winter nights ; how
insufferably suffocating and sickening in the sultry
nights of July and August!
Let us for a moment think of this startling
and ghastly light penetrating the innumerable
dingy streets and back alleys to he found
north, south, and east, in this mighty metro-
polis, inhabited by men and women, ignorant,
dirty, ragged, despairing, or maddened.
Heathens and savages in the worst sense of
the words, and happily so for them, for did a
proper sense of decency or duty exist in such
dens, their inmates could scarce refrain from
cursing the great Author of their existence.
But, above all things, let us think of the little
children born in such horrible places, who
know not why they are there, and who have no
chance of knowing how they may struggle to
liberate themselves from such a diabolical
bondage.

When these things were seen awl fittingly
thought of, the lime-light might travel west-
wards, and allow the eye to penetrate the
mansions of the powerful and the wealthy.
Carpetted,well-lighted, richly-furnished rooms,
gorgeous menials, the rich steams of savoury

dishes, the delicate aro- ma of costly wines, the
bewitching tones of the daintily touched instru-
ment, and, to crown all, the happiness and con-
tentment of those for whom these things exist.
Men and women who waste more in thought-
less riot, in sinful debaucheries, in ridiculous
vanities, than, if rightly applied, would relieve
the worst miseries of those who stiffer most.
Against the right use of riches, or against the
comfort and happiness they bring to their
possessors, nothing need or ought to be said.
But, at the same time, the thoughtlessness,
folly, and wickedness that waste them in riot
aud debauchery, whilst men, women, and
children rot in ignorance and poverty, are sins
which, if not pointed out and corrected, may
some day bring a terrible punishment on the
nation.

We do not wish this light to be thrown into
our fashionable churches and chapels, where
preachers, with gently modulated tones and
soothing phrases, descant on sins which in
their inward consciences they scarce condemn;
and where, to utter the grand words spoken
on behalf of the poor by the founder of their
faith, would be. to shock the nerves of their
sensitive auditors. Here the light is not
wanted. In fact it is needed nowhere. Those
who wish to reform the poor should not think
of making it a part of their attractions when
they call their unfortunate brethren together.
It should be their policy rather to keep such
things in darkness. Those who suffer, and
those who sympathize, should not be asked to
look at these things under too strong a light;
—" that way madness lies," at least, there is
a terrible danger in such revelations. .

THE GENERAL ELECTION AND THE
DIRECT REPRESENTATION OF
LABOUR.
THE London correspondent of the Manches-
ter Guardian in his letter to that paper on
Thursday lasl has collected some curious state.
.ments about labour candidates at the next
general election. We reprint them for the
sake of showing the interest which the subject
is creating :
Indications are not wanting that the machinery
of the various trade societies may have an im-
portant influence in the next general election.
Their excellent organisation for maintaining
the interest of labour in its disputes against
capital has been fully established by many suc-
cesses in recent trade disputes whenever the
working class has been supported by the trade
unions. The introduction of the Ballot into
our electoral system has placed a formidable
machinery in the hands of the labour class,
and it is evident that it will be made the most
of in future parliamentary 'elections. It has
already become a serious consideration among
Liberals whose influence has hitherto controlled
many an election to what extent this new de-
velopment may be used for party purposes. The
leaders of the trade societies are by no means
satisfied with the prospect which at present
appears to await them. Though still loyal to the
present Government, they seem to fear that unless
an early understanding is come to respecting
the plan of the next general campaign they
may find themselves contesting Beata which
are at proaent held by some of Mr. Gladstone's
supporters. On the other hand, it is a fair
question how far the best friends of the Go-
vernment cm treat with or encourage a piov,e-
ment hieh is likely to lead to the
,introduc-
tion of an entirely new element into the House of
'Commons. While this' point is agitating the
minds of some whose tact and influence have
decided the fate of many a contest in favour of
the Liberal cause, the working men are not
neglecting to prepare for whatever contingency
may arise.
In view of the approaching Labour Representa-
tion Conference, which is to be held next month,
it may be useful to indicate who are the candidates
likely to be accepted by the trade societies, or
who have already expressed their intention of
appearing upon the scene at the next general
election. Among the number we may take the
first as Mr. R. M. Latham, the president of the
Labour Representation League. It is in that
capacity that he claims to be a working man's
candidate, for by birth and education he is far
above what is considered as the labour class. By
marriage and property he has already a good cou.
nection with the borough of Wigan, and he is
looked upon as a candidate for that place, instead
of Mr. Pickard, a miner, who it was generally
thought would contest the borough in the interest
of the colliers.

Nov. 30, 1872.

Next to Mr. Latham, by an importance which
is possibly more assumed than acknowledged
among the working classes, save a very small
section, is Mr. G. Odger. Mr. Odger has declared
his intention to stand for Southwark; but bore he
will most likely be opposed by a Mr. Joseph
Leicester, a working glassblower, and who is
well known in that borough as a temperance
advocate. It is not at all improbable that at the
last moment Mr. Odger will find some other fiel
for his activity. There are indications of this in
the visits which he has made to some of the pro-
vineial towns, and notably to Liverpool ; but
wherever he goes he is not likely to have OW
general support of the trade unionists, and hence
he will take his stand rather as a Republican caw
didate than as a representative of labour.
Mr. G. Howell will stand for Aylesbury, whim)
he was a candidate at the last election. I believe
that this course has been taken in consequence ot
a recent manifestation in his favour by his former
supporters.
Mr. George Potter does not seem to have deli-
nitely fixed his intentions; but the two cootests
for the School Board and certain cirourastances
connected with the establishment of the Liberal
Aszociation seem to point to the ancient city of
Westminster as the object of his wooing. He
has nevertheless made many good friends at
Coventry, and he may be heard of in that
borough.
Mr. Robert Applegarth has been frequently
spoken of as a future candidate for Sheffield, where
he passed several years of his life; but the borough _
I of Hull is more likely to be his choice.
Mr. Alexander Macdonald will contest ono of
the mining constituencies, and it is thought that
he will give his preference to a Scottish borough.
Mr. Thomas Burt will endeavour to win Mot.-.
peth from Sir G. Grey, notwithstanding the recent
decision with regard to miners' votes in that
borough.
Mr. John Kane, of Darlington, will, it is thought,
try his fortune at Wednesbury ; and another
miners' candidate will be Mr. Thomas Halliday
at Merthyr. His prospects are looked upon as ex-
ceedingly promising.
Mr. A. Walton is moving in the borough of
Stoke-upon-Trent, and, notwithstanding the fiasco
which was brought about in that town at the last
election by another labour candidate, his chances
of success are deemed by some of the loctal work-
ing men to be very good.
It does not appear that Mr. Cramer has yet
fixed upon what he may hope to make his future
seat, and whether he may once more try.at War-
wick is yet uncertain.
Other working class candidates are also prepar-
ing to take the field, but at present there is a hazy
uncertainty both as to persons and places.
We have no hesitation in saying that the
whole of the above is very hazy indeed.

articles.title: LAND TENURE REFORM.
articles.text:
LAND TENURE REFORM.

On Wednesday evening a meeting was held in
the Lecture Hall of the Mechanics' Institute,
Bradford, under the auspices of the Land Tenure
Reform Association. The attendance was mode-
rate. The Association was represented by a depu-
tation, consisting of Mr. J. Cl. Cox, J.P., of Belper,
Mr. Joseph Arch, president of the Agricultural
Labourers' Society, and Mr. Howard Evans, secre-
tary of the Association. Alderman Law °coupled
the chair.
Mr. Cox moved the following resolution :
That the rights of landed proprietors, which,
being the creation of law, can only be sustained as
means to the general good, are -so interpreted in
existing legislation that this object is greatly
sacrificed to the wealth and importance of a class;
and that the law of landed tenure, and the practice
of Parliament with respect to the land, require
such alterations as may bring them back to their
legitimate purpose. •
Mr. John Rawson seconded the motion.
Mr. Joseph Arch, who was received with several
rounds of applause, supported the resolution.
If anyone had a reason to complain of land
tenure it was the labourers nn the land. They
were a down-trodden lot of men, as was shown by
the low wages they were receiving. In • Dorset-
shire, at the present time, the farmers were offer-
ing their labourers Bs.a week.
Mr. A. Sharp having also supported the motion,
it was carried unanimously.
Mr. Evans moved the next resolution :

That this meeting pledges its hearty support to
i
the Land Tenure Reform Association n its efforts
to secure a settlement of the land question in the
interests of the people.
Mr. Kiddie seconded the motion, and the resolu-
tion was then agreed to.

THE CRIMINAL LAM AMENDMENT ACT.
The Builders' Trades Circular, the organ of the
Master Builders, in its issue of this week makes
the following remarks on the Criminal Law
Amendment Act.—

"Who is not nauseated by the incoherent
rhapsodies of the self-appointed benefactors of the
working classes, and who is not irritated by the
yards of false reasoning which they tell out? We
have long ago given up all hope of the working
classes becoming disgusted by the twaddle which
their mouthy leaders mouth. We are disgusted
nevertheless, and out of our disgust we write.
These precious working classes upon who'll phil-
anthropists and blue stockings so dote, and whose
depraved condition statesmen so deeply deplore,
are agitating for the repeal of the Criminal Law
Amendment Act. This is an Act which puts an
effectual cheek upon the habit wkich unionists had
acquired of beating men whom they choose to
designateblaeksheep, because they choose to accept
terms which the unionists will not. The only
tangible argument which is brought against
this law by those whom it affects is that it is
very difficult to define what moral persuasion is—
to which men are restricted when they Wish to
remove blacksheep from their work—or in other
words induce them to break a legal engagement.
To our mind it is as criminal to induce a man to
break a legal covenant every bit as much as it is
criminal in a man to break an agreement of that
character. But this law would seem to permit one
man to persuade another to do this, inasmuch as it
restrictshira to its use and prohibits him from using
physical force. But, says the man, it is difficult to
aefine " moral suasion." No competent magistrates
have yet found any difficulty in the matter. When-
ever a case has come before a qualified Bench the
"moral suasion" has been so very much akin to
threats of physical force that those who have used
it have either been cautioned as to their behaviour
or convicted for using arguments of a nature not
included in any code of moral law, and therefore
it behoves the building trade generally, who aro
very largely affected by the provisions of this law,
to do their utmost to tetain it upon the statute
book.

MEN OF GLASGOW.

The Secretary to the Glasgow Working Men's
Conservative Association has received the follow-
ing letter from the Right Hon. Benjamin Disraeli:
—" Hughenden Manor, Nov. 22, 1872.—Sir,—I
am highly honoured by the memorial which you
have forwarded to me, requesting that I should
receive an address from the Glasgow Conservative
Working Men's Association on the occasion of my
approaching installation as Lord Rector of the
University. Although lam at all times reluctant
to express my opinions on public affairs except in
ray place in l'arliament, or to those who send me
there, I would not have hesitated to communicate
with the working men of Glasgow had my presence
in their city been occasioned by any political
cause. But that is not the case. The University
has conferred on me a great distinction, of which
I wish to show myself sensible, though at the
cost at this moment of great personal inconveni-
ence. lily visit to the city will be limited to the
fulfilment of a great public duty, and I am there-
fore under the necessity of declining a mark of
respect from the working men of Glasgow, which
I entirely appreciate, and which is offered by
those with whose wishes, under different circum-
stances, I should have been gratiffed in complying.
—I have the honour to remain, Sir, your faithful
servant, B. DISILIABLI."-

articles.text:
REPUBLIC OF LIBERIA.

The Hon. Mrs. Roye (widow of the late
President of Liberia), who left Mr. Chinery's
residence in Willesden-lane about two months
since, on a tour of visits, arrived at the "Gol-
den Cross Hotel," Charing Cross, on Saturday
last, accompanied by her daughter, the Hon.
Miss Roye, and attended by the Rev. G. W.
Gibson, of Monrovia. The distinguished party,
In company with Mr. Chinery, visited the
Bank of England, the Guildhall, and the
Mansion House, on Saturday afternoon; and
on Monday they were entertained at dinner by
Mr. Samuel Gurney, at his residence in the
Regent's Park, returning to Mr. Chinery's in
the evening, where a large number of ladies
and gentlemen assembled to pay their res-
peots to the lion. lady, as well as to mark
their regard for the memory, of the murdered
president. Without fear of contradiction we
may say that Bosworth Lodge was never the
scene of a more enthusiastic and delightful
meeting. The house was crowded with visi-
tors in every available part, amongst the
which were the Hon E. F. Roye, the Rev. G.
W. Gibson, Major and Mrs. Sims, Mr. Digby
Seymour, Q.C., and Mrs. Digby Seymour, Mi.
and Mrs. Walter Wood, Mr. and Mrs. Keeling,
Mr, E. Williams, F.S.A.' and many others.
During the evening Mr. Digby Seymour
delivered an eloquent and touching address.
He said that notwithstanding the treatment
to which the friends of the late president of
Liberia, in 4lonrovia, as well as Mr. Chinery
in this country, had been subjected, there was
an nntrodden future in which the friends with
one united and determined resolution intended
to work. The late preeident had been falsely
charged, for instead of trying him before the
chief justice of the Republic ho was tried
before a judge of the petty sessions; and, hard
as it may be for the people of England to
believe it, it is nevertheless the fact that the
chief witness who gave evidence against him
on his trial was the foreman of the Jury who
tried him. He begged the friends of Liberia
in England and everywhere to wait and watch
for his part. He entirely coincided with his
friend, David Chinery, in his belief that neither
Mr. Roberts or the present Secretary of State
could have been privy to such fearful proceed-
ings as have recently occurred in Monrovia,
or willing advocates of the legal proceedings
now going on in this country, at a fearful
expense to the Government of Liberia. It was
a disgrace to those who professed good intent-
ions towards the little Republic, but who really
knew nothing at all about it, that they did
not yield to the unanimous opinion of Liberia's
real and tried friends, and put an end to the
sxpessive and unnecessary proceedings. A
upbuilding of such men as Gerard Ralston,
Samuel Gurney, and David Chinery, would be
in vain if a change did not come are long in
the policy of the Executive in this country.
He would like to hoar a few words from the
Rev. Mr. Gibson, who had recently arrived
from Liberia.

That gentleman, in the course of an inte-
resting address, said, in reference to the policy
now being exercised in this country,
.that a,
weak government, just struggling into exist-
ence, could not afford expensivelawsuits in the
courts of Great Britain; and if they were
pecuniarily able to afford it they could not
afford to dispense with old and tried friends.
They needed to court, by every method oe-
Bible, friendly aid and co-operation.
Mr. Chinery, Mr: Wood, Mr. Tilley, and
others, delivered addresses during the evening.

The Pope has had losses, and is sadly in
want of money; yet he has just refused
£120,000, or rather a capital sum, invested
in the Italian Funds, bearing that amount of
interest annually! Such stoicism has not
been witnessed since the decay of the Roman
Empire. Of course the reason of the refusal
is that his Holiness forswears the kingdom of
Italy and all its works, the Papal Guarantees
Bill included. Should the sum be refused
for five consecutive years, it will revert to the
Italian Exchequer.
